facts.fact: Edmund Gettier's 1963 paper gave short examples in which a person has a belief that is true and well supported by evidence, yet only true by luck; it argued that 'justified true belief' is therefore not enough to count as knowledge.
facts.hook: a student whose correct answer turns out to have been right for the wrong reason

facts.fact: Philippa Foot's trolley problem asks whether it is permissible to divert a runaway trolley so that it kills one person instead of five; a later variant asks whether it is permissible to push a large person off a bridge to stop it. Most people who answer say yes to the first and no to the second.
facts.hook: two friends who agree on the switch but split over the bridge

facts.fact: Karl Popper argued that a theory counts as scientific only if some possible observation could show it false, and that a theory compatible with every possible outcome tells us nothing.
facts.hook: a club member whose prediction is worded so it can never be wrong

facts.fact: Utilitarianism, as stated by Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill, holds that the right action is the one producing the greatest total happiness, counting each person's happiness equally regardless of who they are.
facts.hook: a class treasurer who must decide whom the last of the budget should help

facts.fact: Immanuel Kant's categorical imperative says to act only on a rule you could will everyone to follow; on this view lying is wrong even to a would-be murderer asking where a friend is hiding, because a universal rule of lying would defeat itself.
facts.hook: a teenager who refuses to tell a protective lie and must live with the result

facts.fact: David Hume observed that no set of statements about what is the case can by itself entail a statement about what ought to be the case; this gap is called the is-ought problem.
facts.hook: a debater who lists facts and expects the moral conclusion to follow

facts.fact: Hume's problem of induction points out that our expectation that the future will resemble the past cannot be justified by past experience without circularity, because that expectation is exactly what is in question.
facts.hook: a student who trusts that the bus is always late because it always has been

facts.fact: John Rawls proposed the 'veil of ignorance': to test whether a social arrangement is fair, imagine choosing it without knowing which position in society you would occupy.
facts.hook: a committee designing prize rules before anyone knows who will compete

facts.fact: John Searle's Chinese Room argument imagines a person who follows a rulebook to answer questions written in Chinese without understanding any of it; Searle used this to argue that manipulating symbols correctly is not the same as understanding them.
facts.hook: a student who aces a test by pattern-matching and is asked to explain one answer

facts.fact: The Ship of Theseus puzzle asks whether a ship whose planks are replaced one by one over the years is still the same ship, and what happens if the old planks are reassembled into a second ship.
facts.hook: a family arguing whether a fully rebuilt cabin is still grandfather's cabin

facts.fact: Descartes argued in his Meditations that even if all his senses deceived him, the act of doubting proved that he existed as a thinking thing, summarized as 'I think, therefore I am'.
facts.hook: someone testing what they could still be sure of after a vivid, convincing dream

facts.fact: Robert Nozick's 'experience machine' thought experiment asks whether you would plug into a machine that gives a lifetime of perfectly pleasant experiences that feel real; he used the common refusal to argue that people value more than pleasant experience.
facts.hook: a gamer offered a flawless simulated life and a reason to say no

facts.fact: Plato's Euthyphro dilemma asks whether something is good because the gods approve it, or whether the gods approve it because it is good; each answer raises a problem for grounding morality in divine command.
facts.hook: a student asking a mentor whether a rule is right only because the mentor said so

facts.fact: Frank Jackson's 'Mary's room' thought experiment describes a scientist who knows every physical fact about color while living in a black-and-white room; it asks whether she learns something new when she first sees red.
facts.hook: a colorblind character who has memorized every fact about a color they cannot see

facts.fact: The 'moral luck' problem, discussed by Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel, notes that two drivers who are equally careless are judged very differently if a child happens to step in front of only one of them, even though the difference was outside their control.
facts.hook: two friends who made the same reckless choice but only one got caught by chance

facts.fact: Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative given up when a choice is made; a free concert still costs an evening that could have been spent otherwise.
facts.hook: a student who takes every free offer and wonders where the time went

facts.fact: A 'sunk cost' is money or effort already spent that cannot be recovered; economists hold that it should not affect a decision about what to do next, yet people routinely keep going because of what they have already put in.
facts.hook: a team that keeps a failing project alive because of the months already spent

facts.fact: Inflation compounds: at 3 percent a year, prices roughly double in about 24 years, so a fixed sum of money buys about half as much over that span.
facts.hook: a grandparent's frozen allowance that once bought far more

facts.fact: The 'tragedy of the commons', described by Garrett Hardin in 1968, is the pattern in which each user of a shared resource gains by taking more while the cost of overuse is spread across everyone, so the resource is depleted.
facts.hook: roommates sharing a fridge that is always empty

facts.fact: A price ceiling set below the market price, such as a strict rent cap, tends to produce shortages because demand rises while the quantity offered falls.
facts.hook: a town where the cheap regulated apartments are all mysteriously full

facts.fact: Comparative advantage, described by David Ricardo, shows that two parties both gain from trade even when one of them is better at producing everything, as long as each specializes in what it gives up least to make.
facts.hook: a star student who does all the group's work and finishes last

facts.fact: The Consumer Price Index measures inflation by tracking the cost of a fixed basket of goods and services over time, and countries periodically update the basket as spending habits change.
facts.hook: a class project that finds grandma's price memories are all in a different basket

facts.fact: A negative externality is a cost imposed on people outside a transaction, such as noise or pollution; a Pigouvian tax, named after Arthur Pigou, is a tax set equal to that outside cost so the price reflects it.
facts.hook: a lemonade stand whose music annoys the whole street

facts.fact: In a bank run, depositors withdraw money because they fear the bank will fail, and because banks hold only a fraction of deposits as cash, the fear itself can cause the failure. Deposit insurance was introduced in many countries to stop this cycle.
facts.hook: a rumor at school that the snack fund is empty makes it empty

facts.fact: Compound interest means interest earns interest; a rule of thumb called the Rule of 72 says money roughly doubles in 72 divided by the annual percentage rate years, so 6 percent doubles in about 12 years.
facts.hook: two siblings who start saving ten years apart

facts.fact: Moral hazard is the tendency to take more risk when someone else bears the cost, such as driving less carefully after buying full insurance coverage.
facts.hook: a borrowed car and a friend who suddenly drives faster

facts.fact: Central banks raise interest rates to slow inflation by making borrowing more expensive, which reduces spending; the effect on prices typically takes a year or more to fully appear.
facts.hook: a student who expects a rate hike to fix prices by next month

facts.fact: Adverse selection occurs when one side of a deal knows more than the other; George Akerlof's 1970 'market for lemons' paper showed that if buyers cannot tell good used cars from bad, good cars tend to be driven out of the market.
facts.hook: a teenager trying to sell a genuinely good used bike and being disbelieved

facts.fact: GDP counts the market value of goods and services produced in a country in a year, but it leaves out unpaid work such as caring for family members and cooking at home.
facts.hook: a student who calculates how much their parent's unpaid work would cost to replace

facts.fact: A progressive income tax with brackets applies the higher rate only to the income above each threshold, so earning one extra dollar over a bracket line never reduces total take-home pay.
facts.hook: a worker who refuses a raise for fear of a higher bracket

facts.fact: A randomized controlled trial assigns participants to treatment or control by chance so that unknown differences between people are spread evenly, which is what lets the result be read as cause rather than mere association.
facts.hook: a student whose study lets volunteers choose their own group

facts.fact: In a double-blind trial neither participants nor the researchers assessing them know who received the real treatment, which prevents expectations from shaping the reported results.
facts.hook: a science fair judge who knows which plant got the fertilizer

facts.fact: The placebo effect is measurable: in many pain trials, a large share of people given an inert pill report real improvement, which is why new drugs must beat placebo, not just do better than nothing.
facts.hook: a sugar pill that seems to cure a friend's headache

facts.fact: The 'replication crisis' refers to the finding that many published psychology results failed to reproduce; a 2015 project that repeated 100 studies found only about a third to a half of the effects held up.
facts.hook: a teacher who cites a famous experiment that has since failed to replicate

facts.fact: Regression to the mean means that an extreme measurement tends to be followed by a more ordinary one by chance alone, so a treatment given after a very bad day can look effective when nothing was done.
facts.hook: a coach who yells after a bad game and credits the yelling for the next win

facts.fact: Ignaz Semmelweis showed in the 1840s that handwashing with chlorinated lime sharply cut deaths from childbed fever in a Vienna maternity clinic, but his finding was rejected for decades partly because he could not explain the mechanism.
facts.hook: someone whose method clearly works but who cannot say why

facts.fact: Newton's law of gravity predicted the orbits of the planets almost perfectly but could not account for a tiny drift in Mercury's orbit of about 43 arcseconds per century, which Einstein's general relativity explained in 1915.
facts.hook: a small stubborn error in the data that turns out to matter most

facts.fact: Peer review means that other experts check a paper before it is published, but reviewers usually do not repeat the experiments or inspect raw data, so peer review catches reasoning errors more reliably than fraud.
facts.hook: a student who believes 'peer-reviewed' means 'proven'

facts.fact: A confounding variable is a hidden factor that affects both things being compared; ice cream sales and drowning rise together each year because both increase in hot weather, not because one causes the other.
facts.hook: a data project that 'proves' something silly

facts.fact: Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912 based on matching coastlines and fossils, but the idea was widely rejected until the 1960s when seafloor spreading supplied a mechanism.
facts.hook: an idea that is right but arrives fifty years before its proof

facts.fact: The Hawthorne effect is the tendency of people to change their behavior simply because they know they are being observed, named after studies at a factory in the 1920s and 1930s.
facts.hook: a survey of classroom behavior that changes the behavior it measures

facts.fact: Survivorship bias is the error of studying only the cases that made it through some filter; during the Second World War, statistician Abraham Wald argued that returning bombers should be armored where they had no bullet holes, since planes hit there did not return.
facts.hook: a student who studies only successful dropouts to prove school is unnecessary

facts.fact: Thomas Kuhn's 1962 book The Structure of Scientific Revolutions argued that science normally works within an accepted framework, or paradigm, and that major changes happen when accumulating anomalies force a shift to a new one.
facts.hook: a lab where everyone explains away the same odd result

facts.fact: The link between smoking and lung cancer was established without a randomized trial, through large cohort studies such as the British Doctors Study begun in 1951, which followed about 40,000 doctors for decades.
facts.hook: a skeptic who says nothing counts without a controlled experiment

facts.fact: Cold fusion was announced at a press conference in 1989 before peer review; laboratories around the world tried and failed to reproduce it within months, and the claim collapsed.
facts.hook: a classmate who announces a discovery before anyone can check it

facts.fact: The Black Death of 1347 to 1351 killed roughly a third or more of Europe's population, and the resulting labor shortage raised wages for surviving peasants and weakened the feudal system.
facts.hook: a character who realizes a catastrophe changed who held the bargaining power

facts.fact: The Rosetta Stone, found in 1799, carries the same decree in Greek and two Egyptian scripts, and comparing them let Jean-Francois Champollion decipher hieroglyphs in 1822.
facts.hook: someone cracking a code because the same message exists in a known language

facts.fact: Radiocarbon dating works because living things absorb carbon-14 that decays at a known rate after death, with a half-life of about 5,730 years; it is useful for objects up to roughly 50,000 years old.
facts.hook: a family heirloom whose claimed age can actually be tested

facts.fact: Dendrochronology dates wood by matching its pattern of wide and narrow annual rings to master sequences built from overlapping samples, which can give an exact year for when a tree was felled.
facts.hook: a beam in an old barn that reveals the true construction date

facts.fact: The Roman numeral system had no zero, and the concept of zero as a number in its own right developed in India, appearing in Brahmagupta's work in the seventh century.
facts.hook: a student who assumes counting has always worked the same way

facts.fact: The 1918 influenza pandemic killed an estimated 50 million people worldwide, more than the First World War, yet it received far less attention in most histories of the period for decades.
facts.hook: someone discovering an ancestor's death was part of a forgotten catastrophe

facts.fact: The 'Great Man' theory, associated with Thomas Carlyle, explains history mainly through the actions of exceptional individuals; later historians such as those of the Annales school instead emphasized long-term economic, geographic and social structures.
facts.hook: two students arguing whether one leader or the weather decided a war

facts.fact: Herodotus, writing in the fifth century BCE, is often called the first historian because he collected accounts from many informants and sometimes reported versions he doubted, telling readers he did not believe them.
facts.hook: a reporter who prints a rumor while stating openly that it may be false

facts.fact: The printing press with movable metal type, developed by Johannes Gutenberg around 1450, dropped the cost of books so much that Europe had an estimated 20 million printed volumes by 1500.
facts.hook: a character imagining a world where every copy of a book is made by hand

facts.fact: The Columbian Exchange after 1492 moved crops between hemispheres: potatoes, tomatoes, maize and chili peppers came from the Americas, so Italian cooking had no tomatoes and Irish farming no potatoes before then.
facts.hook: a student trying to cook a 'traditional' meal without New World ingredients

facts.fact: Oral history projects record interviews with living witnesses, and historians treat them carefully because memory changes over time and people tend to reshape past events in light of what happened later.
facts.hook: two relatives who remember the same family event differently

facts.fact: In 1582 the Gregorian calendar reform skipped ten days, so in the countries that adopted it first, October 4 was followed directly by October 15; Britain did not switch until 1752, when it dropped eleven days.
facts.hook: a diary date that seems impossible until the calendar change is known

facts.fact: The Hittites, who ruled a major empire in Anatolia around 1600 to 1200 BCE, were almost entirely forgotten until their capital and archives of clay tablets were excavated in the early twentieth century.
facts.hook: a character who realizes whole empires can vanish from memory

facts.fact: Ancient Roman concrete, made with volcanic ash, has survived two thousand years in seawater, and researchers have found that it slowly forms new crystals that seal cracks, which is why some harbor structures still stand.
facts.hook: an engineer studying why the old pier outlasted the new one

facts.fact: In a room of just 23 people there is a better than even chance that two share a birthday, because there are 253 different pairs of people that could match.
facts.hook: a student who bets against a birthday match in a small class

facts.fact: The gambler's fallacy is the belief that after a run of one outcome the opposite becomes more likely; a fair coin that has landed heads five times in a row still has exactly a 50 percent chance of heads on the next flip.
facts.hook: a player who is sure the losing streak must end now

facts.fact: Simpson's paradox is when a trend that appears in every subgroup reverses when the groups are combined; a treatment can have a better success rate for both mild and severe cases yet a worse overall rate if it was given mostly to severe cases.
facts.hook: a coach whose player is better in every category but worse overall

facts.fact: A margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points in a poll typically describes a 95 percent confidence interval, meaning that about one poll in twenty would be expected to miss the true value by more than that even with perfect sampling.
facts.hook: a class election poll that is 'wrong' though nothing went wrong

facts.fact: The median is the middle value when data are sorted, and it is unaffected by extreme values; a single billionaire moving into a small town raises the mean income dramatically while barely changing the median.
facts.hook: a report on 'average' pay that hides what most workers earn

facts.fact: Relative risk and absolute risk say different things: a treatment that halves a risk from 2 in 1,000 to 1 in 1,000 is a 50 percent reduction, but only one person in a thousand actually benefits.
facts.hook: a headline about a '50 percent' effect that turns out to be tiny

facts.fact: The law of large numbers says that the average of many independent trials gets closer to the expected value as the number of trials grows, which is why casinos and insurers profit reliably despite individual losses.
facts.hook: a student who wins early at a game and assumes the odds favor them

facts.fact: Bayes' theorem gives a way to update a probability when new evidence arrives, combining how likely the evidence would be if a hypothesis were true with how likely the hypothesis was beforehand.
facts.hook: a detective who revises a suspicion as each clue arrives

facts.fact: The prosecutor's fallacy confuses the chance of the evidence given innocence with the chance of innocence given the evidence; a DNA match that would occur in 1 in a million people could still fit several people in a city of many millions.
facts.hook: a mock trial where one-in-a-million is treated as certainty

facts.fact: Statistical significance at the 5 percent level means that a result this strong would arise by chance about one time in twenty if there were no real effect; it does not mean the effect is large or important.
facts.hook: a science fair project with a significant but useless result

facts.fact: If a researcher tests twenty unrelated hypotheses at the 5 percent significance level, the chance that at least one gives a false positive is about 64 percent, which is why searching many comparisons and reporting the best is misleading.
facts.hook: a student who checks fifty foods against test scores and finds one that 'works'

facts.fact: The expected value of a bet is the average result over many repetitions; a lottery ticket that costs 2 dollars with a one-in-a-million chance at 1 million dollars has an expected value of about 1 dollar, so the buyer loses about half the cost on average.
facts.hook: a student who calculates the school raffle's true payout

facts.fact: Base rates matter for risk: because far more people drive than fly, driving produces many more deaths per year, and per kilometer traveled commercial flying is among the safest ways to travel.
facts.hook: a nervous flyer who drives eight hours to avoid a one-hour flight

facts.fact: Correlation coefficients run from -1 to 1 and measure how closely two variables move together in a straight line; a coefficient of zero can still hide a strong curved relationship.
facts.hook: a data project that reports 'no relationship' for a perfect U-shaped one

facts.fact: The first web page went online in 1991 at CERN, and the World Wide Web's inventor, Tim Berners-Lee, persuaded the lab to release the underlying technology royalty-free in 1993.
facts.hook: a student who learns the web could have been a paid product

facts.fact: Public-key encryption uses a pair of keys: anyone can lock a message with the public key, but only the matching private key can unlock it, which is how a browser can talk securely to a site it has never contacted before.
facts.hook: a class trying to send secret notes without ever meeting to share a password

facts.fact: Recommendation systems on video and social platforms typically optimize for measurable engagement such as watch time and clicks, and content that provokes strong reactions often scores highly on those measures.
facts.hook: a teen who notices their feed gets angrier the more they scroll

facts.fact: A 2018 study in Science that traced about 126,000 stories on Twitter found that false news spread farther and faster than true news, and that humans rather than bots were mainly responsible.
facts.hook: a rumor that beats the correction to every phone in school

facts.fact: GPS receivers calculate position by timing signals from at least four satellites, and the satellite clocks must be corrected for relativity, which makes them run about 38 microseconds a day fast relative to clocks on the ground; without the correction, position errors would grow by kilometers each day.
facts.hook: a hiker who trusts a map app without knowing Einstein is in the loop

facts.fact: Deleting a file usually just marks its storage space as available; the data remains on the disk until overwritten, which is why recovery tools can often retrieve 'deleted' files.
facts.hook: a secret that is deleted but not gone

facts.fact: The Luddites were English textile workers in the 1810s who broke knitting and weaving machines that threatened their skilled jobs; the term is now used, often unfairly, for anyone who resists new technology.
facts.hook: a worker whose objection to a machine is about wages, not fear

facts.fact: Machine-learning systems trained on past data reproduce patterns in that data, so a hiring tool trained on a decade of mostly male hires was found to downgrade resumes containing the word 'women's'.
facts.hook: a school app that ranks students by patterns nobody chose

facts.fact: The first mobile phone call was made in 1973 on a Motorola prototype that weighed about 1.1 kilograms, and consumer models a decade later sold for nearly 4,000 dollars.
facts.hook: a teen amazed that a phone was once a luxury brick

facts.fact: Websites can identify a returning browser without cookies by 'fingerprinting': combining details such as screen size, fonts, time zone and installed plugins, which together are often unique.
facts.hook: a student who clears cookies and is still recognized

facts.fact: Undersea fiber-optic cables carry the vast majority of intercontinental internet traffic, not satellites; a single modern cable can carry hundreds of terabits per second, and cables are occasionally cut by ship anchors.
facts.hook: a character who assumes an overseas message goes through space

facts.fact: Two-factor authentication requires something you know, like a password, plus something you have, like a phone; it protects against stolen passwords but not against someone who is tricked into approving a login request.
facts.hook: a student who approves a login prompt they did not start

facts.fact: The Dunbar number, proposed by anthropologist Robin Dunbar, suggests humans can maintain roughly 150 stable social relationships, a figure often cited when discussing why huge online friend lists do not feel like friendships.
facts.hook: someone with a thousand followers and no one to call

facts.fact: Automated teller machines were widely predicted to eliminate bank teller jobs, but in the United States the number of tellers actually rose for decades after their introduction, because cheaper branches led banks to open more of them.
facts.hook: a student sure a new machine means their part-time job is doomed

facts.fact: The Sapir-Whorf hypothesis in its strong form claims that language determines thought; most linguists reject that version but accept weaker effects, such as speakers of languages that use compass directions instead of 'left' and 'right' being better at keeping track of orientation.
facts.hook: a friend who never gets lost and speaks a language with no word for 'left'

facts.fact: Paul Grice described conversational implicature: hearers assume speakers are being relevant and informative, so 'some of the students passed' is usually taken to mean not all did, even though it is literally true if all passed.
facts.hook: a reference letter that damns by saying only that the student was punctual

facts.fact: Noam Chomsky's poverty-of-the-stimulus argument holds that children acquire grammar rules they were never explicitly taught and rarely hear violated, which he took as evidence for an inborn language capacity.
facts.hook: a toddler who says 'goed' though no adult ever did

facts.fact: Deaf children in Nicaragua in the 1980s, brought together in schools for the first time, created a new sign language with its own grammar within a generation, and it was the younger children who added the most systematic structure.
facts.hook: a group of kids who invent a language their teachers cannot follow

facts.fact: The McGurk effect shows that seeing a mouth make one sound while hearing another can make listeners perceive a third sound, which demonstrates that speech perception combines vision and hearing.
facts.hook: a video call where the lips and the audio disagree

facts.fact: In Ludwig Wittgenstein's later view, the meaning of a word is its use in a shared practice, and he argued that a purely private language, referring to sensations only its user could check, would be impossible.
facts.hook: a diary code that stops meaning anything even to its author

facts.fact: Ferdinand de Saussure argued that the link between a word's sound and its meaning is arbitrary, which is why 'dog', 'chien' and 'perro' all name the same animal, and only a few words like 'buzz' imitate what they mean.
facts.hook: a student inventing a language and discovering words need not resemble things

facts.fact: The 'Bouba/Kiki' effect is the finding that people across many languages match the nonsense word 'bouba' to a rounded shape and 'kiki' to a spiky one, which suggests some sound-meaning links are not entirely arbitrary.
facts.hook: a class naming products and finding everyone agrees on the spiky one

facts.fact: J. L. Austin's speech-act theory notes that some utterances perform actions rather than describe things: saying 'I promise' or 'I now pronounce you married' under the right conditions makes the promise or the marriage.
facts.hook: a student who says 'I bet you' as a joke and is held to it

facts.fact: The Stroop effect shows that naming the ink color of a word is much slower when the word spells a different color, such as 'red' printed in blue, because reading happens automatically.
facts.hook: a party game that reveals how hard it is not to read

facts.fact: Loftus and Palmer's 1974 experiment found that people who watched a car crash and were asked how fast the cars 'smashed' gave higher speed estimates than those asked how fast the cars 'hit', and were more likely to later recall broken glass that was not there.
facts.hook: a witness whose memory is quietly rewritten by the question

facts.fact: Every language studied so far has a way to express negation, ask questions and refer to past or future events, but there is wide variation elsewhere; some languages have no grammatical tense at all and mark time with separate words.
facts.hook: a student who assumes every language must have verb tenses

facts.fact: Metaphor structures ordinary speech: as George Lakoff and Mark Johnson showed, English routinely treats argument as war ('attack a claim', 'defend a position') and time as money ('spend', 'waste', 'save' time).
facts.hook: a student who tries to argue for a day without any war words

facts.fact: Semantic satiation is the effect in which a word repeated many times seems to lose its meaning and become a mere sound, and it can be produced reliably in about half a minute of repetition.
facts.hook: a chant at a game that turns a word into noise

facts.fact: An argument is valid when it is impossible for all its premises to be true and its conclusion false; validity depends only on the argument's form, not on whether the premises are true.
facts.hook: Two friends at a coffee shop argue over a silly syllogism about dragons, and one insists it is valid even though dragons do not exist.

facts.fact: A deductive argument is called sound only when it is valid and all of its premises are actually true, so a sound argument's conclusion must be true.
facts.hook: A debate-club student realizes her opponent's argument is valid but not sound, because one premise is simply false.

facts.fact: Affirming the consequent is a logical fallacy: from 'if P then Q' and 'Q', concluding 'P'. Living in San Diego means living in California, but living in California does not mean living in San Diego.
facts.hook: At dinner, a sibling says 'if it rained the lawn is wet, the lawn is wet, so it rained,' and someone points to the sprinkler.

facts.fact: A counterfactual conditional describes what would have been true if things had been different, such as 'if Sally owned a donkey, she would ride it', and usually implies the 'if' part is false.
facts.hook: After missing the bus, a teen keeps saying what would have happened if he had left five minutes earlier, and a friend notes he can never check it.

facts.fact: Philosopher Stephen Toulmin, in his 1958 book The Uses of Argument, described an argument's backbone as a claim, the grounds or data supporting it, and a warrant explaining why those grounds support the claim.
facts.hook: A student outlining a persuasive essay realizes her evidence is fine but she never wrote the warrant linking it to her claim.

facts.fact: A straw man is the fallacy of attacking a weaker, distorted version of someone's argument instead of the argument they actually made, while acting as if the two are the same.
facts.hook: In a class discussion, a student notices a classmate rebutting a position nobody in the room actually took.

facts.fact: Steelmanning is the practice of restating an opposing argument in its strongest form, even stronger than the other person put it, before responding to it.
facts.hook: Before arguing with her father about curfew, a teen tries to state his reasons better than he did, and the conversation changes.

facts.fact: A necessary condition must hold for something to happen but may not be enough: the sun being above the horizon is necessary for direct sunlight, but not sufficient, since something may cast a shadow.
facts.hook: Two friends argue whether good grades guarantee admission, and one explains the difference between necessary and sufficient.

facts.fact: In Peter Wason's 1966 selection task, people must pick which cards to turn over to test an if-then rule; in his study, fewer than 10 percent chose the correct cards in the abstract version.
facts.hook: A psychology class tries the four-card puzzle, and almost everyone forgets to check the card that could disprove the rule.

facts.fact: Modus ponens is the valid argument form 'if P then Q; P; therefore Q', and it is valid no matter what P and Q stand for.
facts.hook: A student replaces the words in a logic problem with nonsense words and discovers the argument still works.

facts.fact: Elisabeth Kübler-Ross introduced the five stages of denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance in her 1969 book On Death and Dying, originally to describe terminally ill patients facing their own death.
facts.hook: A teen who feels none of the stages after her grandfather's death learns the model was first written about dying patients, not mourners.

facts.fact: Psychologist George Bonanno's research on bereaved people found that resilience is common, and that there are no mandatory stages that everyone must pass through after a loss.
facts.hook: A grandson worries he is not grieving correctly because he is still going to school and laughing with friends.

facts.fact: Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut's dual process model describes grieving people as moving back and forth between facing the loss and getting on with rebuilding daily life, rather than moving in one direction.
facts.hook: A teen feels guilty for enjoying a movie the week after the funeral, until a relative explains that switching back and forth is normal.

facts.fact: The 1996 book Continuing Bonds, by Dennis Klass, Phyllis Silverman and Steven Nickman, argued that keeping a lasting connection with someone who has died is a normal part of grief, not a failure to move on.
facts.hook: A granddaughter keeps her grandmother's recipe cards and talks to her while cooking, and wonders if that is okay.

facts.fact: Mexico's Day of the Dead is traditionally celebrated on November 1 and 2, when families build ofrendas, or home altars, with photos and the favorite foods and drinks of relatives who have died.
facts.hook: A family decides what to put on the altar for the grandmother who died this year, starting with her favorite sweet bread.

facts.fact: On Mexico's Day of the Dead, orange marigolds called cempasúchil decorate altars and graves, because their bright color and strong scent are thought to guide the souls of the dead home.
facts.hook: Sent to the market for marigolds before the Day of the Dead, a teen asks her aunt why it has to be those flowers.

facts.fact: In Judaism, the closest relatives of the person who died sit shiva, a mourning period of seven days that begins after the burial; the Hebrew word shiva means seven.
facts.hook: A teen visiting a friend's family during shiva wonders what to say and what to bring.

facts.fact: During Japan's Buddhist festival of Obon, families light fires to welcome the spirits of ancestors home, and at the end many float lanterns down rivers to guide the spirits back.
facts.hook: Spending the summer with relatives in Japan, a teen helps set a lantern on the river for the grandfather she barely knew.

facts.fact: During China's Qingming Festival, which falls on April 4, 5 or 6, families visit their ancestors' graves to sweep and clean them and leave offerings of food.
facts.hook: A grandson goes along to sweep his grandfather's grave for the first time and learns why the family goes every spring.

facts.fact: The Common Application, which lets US college applicants send one application to many schools, was founded in 1975 with 15 member colleges and now has more than 1,000 members.
facts.hook: Filling out the Common App at the kitchen table, a senior is relieved she does not have to write twenty separate applications.

facts.fact: Early Decision in US college admissions is binding: a student admitted with acceptable financial aid must enroll and withdraw all other applications.
facts.hook: A senior hesitates to apply Early Decision because she has not seen what financial aid other schools would offer.

facts.fact: Early Action in US college admissions gives an early decision but is non-binding, so an admitted student may still choose not to enroll.
facts.hook: A student gets an early acceptance in December and debates whether to stop applying anywhere else.

facts.fact: In US college admissions, a college's yield is the percentage of students it admits who then accept the offer and enroll.
facts.hook: On a campus tour, a senior hears a guide boast about yield and asks what it means.

facts.fact: Many US colleges fill waitlist spots in May, after admitted students have sent deposits and the college knows how many places are still open.
facts.hook: Waitlisted at her top choice, a senior must decide whether to pay a deposit elsewhere while she waits.

facts.fact: Need-blind admission means a college decides whom to admit without considering whether the applicant can afford to pay; many US colleges are instead need-aware.
facts.hook: A student whose family cannot pay much compares which colleges on her list look at finances when deciding.

facts.fact: The FAFSA is the form US students complete to apply for federal financial aid such as Pell Grants and federal loans, and many states and colleges also use it to award their own aid.
facts.hook: A senior and her mother sit at the computer late at night working through the FAFSA before a state aid deadline.

facts.fact: In the UK, students apply to university through UCAS and can choose up to five courses, listed in no order of preference.
facts.hook: A student applying to British universities struggles to narrow her list of courses down to five.

facts.fact: Starting with applicants for 2026 entry, UCAS replaced the free-form personal statement with three structured questions about why the applicant wants the subject and how they have prepared.
facts.hook: A UK student realizes the essay advice from his older cousin no longer matches the new three-question format.

facts.fact: The SAT switched to a digital, adaptive format in the United States in March 2024: how well a student does on the first module of each section sets the difficulty of the second.
facts.hook: After a hard second math module, a student panics, until a friend explains that harder questions may mean she did well on the first.

facts.fact: In his 1961 book What Is History?, E. H. Carr described history as 'an unending dialogue between the present and the past'.
facts.hook: At a monument, a teen and grandparent disagree about what it means, and the teen wonders whether both readings can count as history.

facts.fact: In 1824 German historian Leopold von Ranke wrote that his work aimed only to show the past 'as it actually was', rather than to judge it or instruct the present.
facts.hook: Writing a history essay, a student asks whether it is even possible to describe the past without taking a side.

facts.fact: In his 1963 book The Making of the English Working Class, E. P. Thompson said he wanted to rescue ordinary workers from 'the enormous condescension of posterity'.
facts.hook: Researching family history, a teen finds his great-great-grandfather was a mill worker who appears in no history book.

facts.fact: In his 1961 book Griff nach der Weltmacht, German historian Fritz Fischer argued that Imperial Germany deliberately pursued a world war, setting off a long debate known as the Fischer controversy.
facts.hook: Two students in a history class find their textbooks give different answers about who caused the First World War.

facts.fact: German historian Alexander Demandt compiled a list of 210 different explanations that writers have offered for why the Western Roman Empire fell.
facts.hook: A student arguing for one cause of Rome's fall is shown just how many other explanations exist.

facts.fact: One Vindolanda tablet is a birthday party invitation from Claudia Severa to Sulpicia Lepidina, written around 100 CE, with closing lines that are among the earliest known Latin writing by a woman.
facts.hook: A student who thought ancient women left no voice is surprised by a Roman birthday invitation.

facts.fact: An argument from silence draws a conclusion from what a source fails to mention; historians treat it with caution because writers record only what seems important to them.
facts.hook: A grandchild says an event never happened because Grandpa's diary does not mention it, and Grandpa laughs.

facts.fact: Historian Frances Wood argued that Marco Polo may never have reached China, pointing out that his book never mentions tea, foot-binding or the Great Wall.
facts.hook: A student doing a report on Marco Polo finds a book questioning whether his famous journey happened at all.

facts.fact: The ancient Greek historian Thucydides admitted that the speeches in his history of the Peloponnesian War were not word-for-word records, but what he judged each speaker would have needed to say.
facts.hook: A student quoting a famous ancient speech learns the historian himself wrote much of it.

facts.fact: A primary source was produced at the time being studied, such as a letter or diary, while a secondary source, such as a textbook, interprets the past later using primary sources.
facts.hook: Sorting a box of a grandparent's wartime letters, a teen realizes she is holding primary sources.

facts.fact: Historiography is the study of how history has been written, including how historians' interpretations of the same events have changed over time.
facts.hook: A student notices her grandmother's school textbook tells the story of a war very differently from her own.

facts.fact: In common-law countries such as the US, UK and Canada, a contract generally needs an offer, an acceptance and consideration, meaning something of value given by each side in exchange.
facts.hook: A teen wonders whether his friend's promise to pay him for tutoring is a real contract.

facts.fact: Under English common law, consideration must have some value but need not be a fair price; courts do not generally judge whether a bargain was a good one.
facts.hook: A teen sells his bike for far less than it is worth and later wonders if he can undo the deal.

facts.fact: In common-law jurisdictions, including most of the US, a contract made by a minor is generally voidable by the minor, with exceptions such as contracts for necessities.
facts.hook: At a gym front desk, a 17-year-old is told he needs a parent's signature on his membership contract.

facts.fact: In the United States, courts generally will not enforce a liability waiver that tries to excuse gross negligence or intentional misconduct, even if the person signed it.
facts.hook: Signing a waiver for a climbing gym, a teen asks what the gym is actually still responsible for.

facts.fact: To indemnify someone is to promise, in a contract, to compensate them for losses they suffer because of certain acts, often written alongside a promise to 'hold harmless'.
facts.hook: Reading a rental form for an event venue, a student stops at the word 'indemnify' and asks what she is agreeing to.

facts.fact: The US ESIGN Act, passed in 2000, says a signature or contract may not be denied legal effect solely because it is in electronic form.
facts.hook: A teen signs a job agreement by clicking on a screen and asks if that really counts as signing.

facts.fact: Under the US Federal Trade Commission's Cooling-Off Rule, buyers can cancel certain sales made at home or at temporary locations until midnight of the third business day after the sale.
facts.hook: A salesperson at a hotel booth talks a teen's parent into a purchase they regret the next morning.

facts.fact: Under the legal rule called contra proferentem, used in many jurisdictions, an ambiguous term in a contract is usually read against the party that wrote it.
facts.hook: A student and a phone company disagree over what an unclear line in the contract means.

facts.fact: A force majeure clause frees the parties from their obligations when an extraordinary event outside their control, such as a natural disaster or war, prevents them from performing.
facts.hook: A concert is canceled after a storm, and a teen reads the ticket terms to see whether she gets a refund.

facts.fact: Informed consent in medicine means a patient agrees to treatment after being told its risks, benefits and alternatives in words they can understand.
facts.hook: At a clinic, a 17-year-old reads a consent form and asks the nurse to explain a risk before signing.

facts.fact: Under joint and several liability, each of several people who share an obligation can be held responsible for the entire amount, not only their own share.
facts.hook: Three friends plan to sign an apartment lease together, and one reads that each could owe the whole rent.

facts.fact: An arbitration clause requires the parties to settle disputes through private arbitration instead of in court, and in the US it is often paired with a waiver of class-action lawsuits.
facts.hook: Scrolling through an app's terms at a computer at home, a teen finds she has agreed not to sue in court.

facts.fact: The Maillard reaction, between amino acids and sugars, browns food and creates much of its flavor; it proceeds rapidly at about 140 to 165 degrees Celsius.
facts.hook: A teen's pale, steamed chicken disappoints the family, and a grandparent explains why the pan needed to be hotter.

facts.fact: Caramelization is the browning of sugar on its own, without proteins; table sugar begins to caramelize at about 170 degrees Celsius.
facts.hook: Making caramel sauce for dessert, a teen watches the sugar change color and debates when to take it off the heat.

facts.fact: US food safety agencies say chicken is safely cooked when its internal temperature reaches 165 degrees Fahrenheit, about 74 degrees Celsius, measured with a food thermometer.
facts.hook: Cooking a family dinner, a teen cuts into a chicken breast to check it, and her dad hands her a thermometer instead.

facts.fact: US food safety guidance says perishable food should not sit between 40 and 140 degrees Fahrenheit for more than two hours, or one hour when it is above 90 degrees.
facts.hook: After a long family cookout, a teen has to decide which leftovers are still safe to save.

facts.fact: The CDC advises against washing raw chicken, because the splashing water can spread bacteria to the sink and nearby surfaces.
facts.hook: A teen starts rinsing chicken in the sink the way a relative always did, and a sibling stops him.

facts.fact: Water boils at a lower temperature at high altitude, about 95 degrees Celsius at 5,000 feet, so boiled foods take longer to cook.
facts.hook: At a mountain campsite, the family's pasta is still hard after the usual cooking time.

facts.fact: Gluten forms when the wheat proteins glutenin and gliadin mix with water, and kneading longer makes the gluten network stronger and the bread chewier.
facts.hook: A first homemade loaf comes out dense and crumbly, and the teen wonders if he kneaded it enough.

facts.fact: In mayonnaise, lecithin and proteins from egg yolk act as emulsifiers, holding tiny oil droplets suspended in water so the sauce does not separate.
facts.hook: A homemade mayonnaise splits into oil and liquid, and a grandparent shows how to rescue it with another yolk.

facts.fact: Carryover cooking means food keeps cooking after it leaves the heat, and a large roast's internal temperature can rise by several degrees while it rests.
facts.hook: A teen pulls a roast out right at the target temperature, and it comes out overcooked after resting.

facts.fact: Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases enzymes that produce syn-propanethial-S-oxide, a vapor that irritates the eyes and makes them tear.
facts.hook: Chopping onions for the family's soup, a teen tears up and her brother teases her for crying.

facts.fact: Mise en place is a French cooking term meaning 'putting in place': measuring and preparing all the ingredients before starting to cook.
facts.hook: Halfway through a recipe, a teen discovers there are no eggs, and learns why cooks set everything out first.

facts.fact: Isaac Newton arranged the colors of the spectrum into a circle in his 1704 book Opticks, an early version of the color wheel artists use today.
facts.hook: Planning a painting's color scheme at the kitchen table, a teen learns the color wheel began with a physicist.

facts.fact: Chemist Michel Eugène Chevreul published his law of simultaneous contrast in 1839, describing how a color appears to shift toward the complement of the color placed next to it.
facts.hook: A teen's gray paint looks warm on one part of her canvas and cool on another, and she wonders why.

facts.fact: Mixing paints is subtractive: each pigment absorbs some wavelengths of light, so mixing many pigments together tends toward a dark, muddy color rather than white.
facts.hook: Trying to mix a bright color, a teen keeps adding paint until it turns brown.

facts.fact: The phrase 'rule of thirds' was first written down by John Thomas Smith in his 1797 book Remarks on Rural Scenery.
facts.hook: A friend at the community art studio tells a teen to put the horizon a third of the way down, and she asks who made that rule.

facts.fact: Around 1420 in Florence, Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrated linear perspective, the technique of drawing lines that meet at a vanishing point to show depth on a flat surface.
facts.hook: A teen's drawing of a hallway looks flat until she adds a vanishing point.

facts.fact: Kintsugi is a Japanese technique of repairing broken pottery with lacquer mixed or dusted with powdered gold, treating the break as part of the object's history rather than hiding it.
facts.hook: A teen accidentally breaks a grandparent's bowl and decides to repair it so the crack shows.

facts.fact: ISO 216 paper sizes such as A4 have sides in the ratio of 1 to the square root of 2, so cutting a sheet in half gives two sheets of the same shape.
facts.hook: Scaling a poster design at a public library printer, a student notices the A3 and A4 versions match perfectly.

facts.fact: A pencil's core is a mix of graphite and clay; more clay makes a harder pencil with lighter marks, marked H, and less clay makes a softer, darker one, marked B.
facts.hook: A teen's sketch smudges everywhere, and a friend asks which pencil grade she used.

facts.fact: Pencil 'lead' has never been made of the metal lead; the name comes from the 16th century, when graphite was mistaken for a kind of lead ore.
facts.hook: A younger cousin worries about lead poisoning after chewing a pencil, and a teen explains what is really inside.

facts.fact: Acrylic paint is water-based while wet, but it dries quickly and becomes water-resistant once dry.
facts.hook: A teen leaves her brushes out during a break and finds them stiff with dried acrylic.

facts.fact: Earthenware pottery is normally fired below about 1,200 degrees Celsius, while porcelain is fired between about 1,200 and 1,400 degrees Celsius.
facts.hook: At a community art studio, a teen learns why her clay and her friend's must go in different kiln loads.

facts.fact: Negative space is the empty area around and between the subjects of an image, and artists often draw that space to get a shape's outline right.
facts.hook: Struggling to draw a chair, a teen tries drawing the gaps between its legs instead.

facts.fact: Braking distance is proportional to the square of speed, so doubling a car's speed makes the distance needed to brake about four times as long.
facts.hook: On a first lesson, the instructor asks a learner to guess how much longer it takes to stop at twice the speed.

facts.fact: Under the two-second rule, a driver watches the car ahead pass a fixed point, such as a sign, and checks that at least two seconds pass before reaching that same point.
facts.hook: A nervous learner keeps creeping up behind other cars until the instructor teaches her to count seconds from a lamppost.

facts.fact: The US National Safety Council recommends a following distance of at least three seconds, adding a second for each difficulty such as bad weather or heavy traffic.
facts.hook: A parent supervising practice says three seconds, while the teen's friend swears by two.

facts.fact: A blind spot is an area around a car the driver cannot see from the seat, even with mirrors, which is why drivers turn their heads to check before changing lanes.
facts.hook: On a first lesson, a learner almost changes lanes into a car hidden beside her.

facts.fact: In a car with anti-lock brakes, a driver in an emergency should press the brake firmly and hold it rather than pump it, and can still steer.
facts.hook: A grandparent tells a learner to pump the brakes, and the instructor explains why that advice is out of date.

facts.fact: In the UK, a driver who passes the test in an automatic car may drive only automatic cars, and must pass a manual test to drive a manual car.
facts.hook: A learner choosing lessons at a driving school weighs the easier automatic against the family's manual car.

facts.fact: According to the CDC, US drivers aged 16 to 19 have a fatal crash rate almost three times as high as drivers aged 20 and older, per mile driven.
facts.hook: At the licensing office, a teen reads a poster about crash risk while waiting for her permit test.

facts.fact: According to the CDC, wearing a seat belt reduces serious crash-related injuries and deaths by about half.
facts.hook: A learner forgets her seat belt in the driveway, and the instructor refuses to start the lesson.

facts.fact: Most US and Canadian jurisdictions use graduated licensing, in which new drivers move from a learner's permit to a provisional license with restrictions before a full license.
facts.hook: A teen who just got his permit is disappointed to learn he cannot drive friends around right away.

facts.fact: Hydroplaning happens when a layer of water builds up between the tires and the road so the car loses traction; easing off the accelerator can let the tires regain grip.
facts.hook: Practicing on a rainy evening, a learner feels the steering go light on a flooded patch of road.

facts.fact: Sociologist Robert K. Merton's 1936 essay 'The Unanticipated Consequences of Purposive Social Action' listed causes of unintended consequences, including ignorance, error and focusing on immediate interests over long-term ones.
facts.hook: A student council's plan to cut cafeteria waste backfires, and a teacher asks the students why they did not see it coming.

facts.fact: In 1902, French colonial authorities in Hanoi paid a bounty for each rat tail, and people began cutting off tails and releasing the rats to breed, so the rat problem grew.
facts.hook: At the dinner table, a teen proposes paying her brother per chore, and her mother tells the rat-tail story.

facts.fact: The doctrine of double effect, traced to Thomas Aquinas, holds that causing a harm one foresees but does not intend can be permissible when it is a side effect of pursuing a good end.
facts.hook: During a hospital volunteer shift, a teen hears a doctor discuss giving pain relief that might shorten a patient's life.

facts.fact: Principle 15 of the 1992 Rio Declaration states that where there are threats of serious or irreversible environmental damage, lack of full scientific certainty should not delay cost-effective preventive measures.
facts.hook: Debating a new pesticide in class, one student says to wait for proof of harm and another cites the precautionary principle.

facts.fact: In Darley and Latané's 1968 experiment, about 85 percent of people who thought they alone heard someone having a seizure helped, but only about 31 percent did when they thought four others heard it.
facts.hook: At a coffee shop, a customer collapses and everyone looks around waiting for someone else to act.

facts.fact: Risk compensation is the tendency of people to behave less carefully when a safety measure makes them feel protected, so the measure can deliver less benefit than predicted.
facts.hook: A friend who just got a new helmet starts riding his bike much faster down the hill.

facts.fact: A Pareto improvement, named after economist Vilfredo Pareto, is a change that makes at least one person better off without making anyone worse off.
facts.hook: Planning how to split a shared car between siblings, a teen looks for a schedule nobody loses under.

facts.fact: In his 1979 book The Imperative of Responsibility, Hans Jonas proposed the rule: 'Act so that the effects of your action are compatible with the permanence of genuine human life.'
facts.hook: Arguing about a new technology at school, a student asks who speaks for people not yet born.

facts.fact: In his Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle described each virtue as a mean between two extremes; courage, for example, lies between cowardice and recklessness.
facts.hook: A teen wonders whether confronting a friend in front of everyone was brave or just reckless.

facts.fact: R. Edward Freeman's 1984 book Strategic Management: A Stakeholder Approach argued that businesses should consider everyone affected by their decisions, not only their owners.
facts.hook: At a part-time job, a teen sees a schedule change that helps the store but hurts workers who take the bus.

facts.fact: Aristotle held that people are responsible for actions done voluntarily, and that actions done under force or through ignorance of the circumstances can be involuntary.
facts.hook: A teen who unknowingly passed on a false rumor wonders how much of the blame is hers.

facts.fact: Many ethicists distinguish doing harm from allowing harm, and most people judge causing a harm as worse than failing to prevent an equal harm, though some philosophers reject the distinction.
facts.hook: At the dinner table, a family argues whether not warning a neighbor is as bad as causing the problem.

facts.fact: The 2018 Gender Shades study by Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru found commercial facial analysis systems had error rates up to 34.7 percent for darker-skinned women but under 1 percent for lighter-skinned men.
facts.hook: A photo app keeps failing to recognize a teen's face while it works instantly for her friend.

facts.fact: A 2016 ProPublica investigation found that the COMPAS risk tool misclassified Black defendants who did not reoffend as high risk at about twice the rate of white defendants.
facts.hook: In a class debate, a student argues computers should decide bail because they are neutral.

facts.fact: A 2019 study led by Ziad Obermeyer found a widely used US health-care algorithm underestimated Black patients' needs because it used past medical spending as a stand-in for how sick patients were.
facts.hook: On a tech company field trip, a student asks how an engineer knows what a data label really measures.

facts.fact: Jeremy Bentham's 1791 panopticon was a prison design with a central tower from which inmates could be watched at any time without knowing whether they were.
facts.hook: A teen notices she behaves differently at work once she learns the security camera might be on.

facts.fact: In his 1975 book Discipline and Punish, Michel Foucault used Bentham's panopticon as a metaphor for how modern institutions control people through the possibility of constant observation.
facts.hook: Students debate whether classroom monitoring software is more like a teacher's glance or a watchtower.

facts.fact: The Collingridge dilemma, from David Collingridge's 1980 book, says a technology's effects are hard to predict when it is new, but by the time they are clear it is hard to change.
facts.hook: Friends at a coffee shop argue whether it is too early or too late to set rules for a new app everyone uses.

facts.fact: A 2013 study by Carl Benedikt Frey and Michael Osborne estimated that 47 percent of US jobs were at high risk of automation.
facts.hook: A teen working a part-time cashier job watches self-checkout machines being installed.

facts.fact: Automation bias is the tendency to favor suggestions from automated systems and to ignore contradicting information, even when that information is correct.
facts.hook: A driver follows a GPS instruction onto a closed road despite the warning signs in front of her.

facts.fact: The European Union's AI Act, which entered into force on August 1, 2024, bans some uses of AI outright, including social scoring of people.
facts.hook: Reading about a school that ranks students by online behavior, a teen asks whether that would be legal in Europe.

facts.fact: In June 2013, documents leaked by Edward Snowden revealed that the US National Security Agency was collecting phone records, such as numbers called and call durations, of millions of Verizon customers.
facts.hook: A teen shrugs that she has nothing to hide, and a friend asks whether she would mind a list of everyone she calls.

facts.fact: In a 1974 study by Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron, men who had just crossed a frightening suspension bridge were more likely to call a female interviewer afterward than men who crossed a sturdy bridge.
facts.hook: Someone wonders whether the pounding heart after a scary movie means they like their date or were just scared.

facts.fact: Psychologists call it misattribution of arousal when a racing heart caused by fear or excitement is mistaken for attraction to the person nearby.
facts.hook: After a tense bowling tiebreaker, a teen tries to sort out whether the jittery feeling is nerves or a crush.

facts.fact: In Arthur Aron's 1997 study, pairs of strangers took turns asking each other 36 questions that grew gradually more personal, and they ended up feeling closer than pairs making small talk.
facts.hook: A date runs out of things to say at the coffee shop and one of them suggests trading harder questions.

facts.fact: In a 1999 study, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh found that people liked a partner more when that partner quietly mimicked their posture and gestures, even without noticing the mimicry.
facts.hook: A teen notices both of them have leaned on their elbows the same way and wonders if that is a good sign.

facts.fact: In a 1966 experiment by Elliot Aronson and colleagues, a highly competent quiz contestant who spilled a cup of coffee was rated more likable afterward; this is called the pratfall effect.
facts.hook: Someone knocks over a drink early in the date and is sure the whole evening is ruined.

facts.fact: A 2018 study by Erica Boothby and colleagues found a liking gap: after a first conversation, people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company.
facts.hook: Walking home, a teen replays every awkward moment and decides the date must have hated it.

facts.fact: In the CDC's 2021 Youth Risk Behavior Survey, about 1 in 12 US high school students who had dated reported experiencing physical dating violence.
facts.hook: A friend notices that someone's new partner keeps grabbing their arm hard and decides to say something.

facts.fact: In the law of many jurisdictions and in consent education, consent to any intimate contact can be withdrawn at any time, even after it was first given.
facts.hook: On the walk to the car, one person says they would rather just say goodnight, and the other has to respect that.

facts.fact: The US federal minimum wage has been $7.25 an hour since July 24, 2009, though many states and cities set a higher minimum.
facts.hook: Two friends compare their first paychecks and cannot understand why one earns more per hour in the next state.

facts.fact: Under US federal child labor rules, workers under 18 may not operate power-driven meat slicers, even in a grocery store deli or restaurant.
facts.hook: A seventeen-year-old new hire is asked to cover the deli slicer and has to say no.

facts.fact: In the United States, every new employee must complete Section 1 of Form I-9, which verifies identity and permission to work, no later than their first day of paid work.
facts.hook: A teen shows up for orientation and is handed a form they have never seen before.

facts.fact: In the United States, a new employee fills out Form W-4 so the employer knows how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck.
facts.hook: A teen stares at the W-4 at the hardware store and texts a parent for help.

facts.fact: US employers withhold 6.2 percent of an employee's wages for Social Security tax, up to a yearly wage limit.
facts.hook: Someone works out why their paycheck is smaller than their hours times their hourly rate.

facts.fact: Under the US Fair Labor Standards Act, non-exempt employees must be paid one and a half times their regular rate for hours worked beyond 40 in a workweek.
facts.hook: A teen picking up extra shifts over break notices a higher rate on some of their hours.

facts.fact: The STAR method answers interview questions about past behavior by describing a Situation, the Task required, the Action you took, and the Result.
facts.hook: Before a coffee shop interview, a teen practices telling the story of a group project that went wrong.

facts.fact: Most US employment is at-will, meaning the employer or the worker can end the job at any time for any reason that is not illegal.
facts.hook: A new hire wonders whether they need to give notice before quitting a job they hate.

facts.fact: Montana is the one US state where, after a probationary period, an employer generally needs good cause to fire a worker, under its 1987 Wrongful Discharge from Employment Act.
facts.hook: Cousins in two states argue about whether a boss can fire someone just for being in a bad mood.

facts.fact: The 26th Amendment, which set the US voting age at 18, was ratified in 1971 in about three months, faster than any other amendment.
facts.hook: At the dinner table a grandparent mentions they could not vote at eighteen, and the new voter is surprised.

facts.fact: Supporters of lowering the US voting age to 18 used the slogan "old enough to fight, old enough to vote," because 18-year-olds could be drafted for the Vietnam War.
facts.hook: An eighteen-year-old wonders aloud why their vote matters, and a relative explains where the right came from.

facts.fact: Canada lowered its federal voting age from 21 to 18 in 1970.
facts.hook: A Canadian teen registering for the first time asks how long people their age have been allowed to vote.

facts.fact: The secret printed ballot is called the Australian ballot because Australian colonies, Tasmania and Victoria, introduced it in 1856.
facts.hook: A first-time voter asks why nobody is allowed to see how they mark their ballot.

facts.fact: North Dakota is the only US state without voter registration; it abolished registration in 1951, and voters instead show identification at the polls.
facts.hook: A student who just moved from North Dakota is confused when told they must register first.

facts.fact: Under the US Help America Vote Act of 2002, a voter whose eligibility is in question can cast a provisional ballot, which counts only once officials confirm eligibility.
facts.hook: A first-time voter's name is not on the list at the community hall and a poll worker offers another option.

facts.fact: An overvote happens when a voter marks more choices than a contest allows, and that vote is not counted for that contest.
facts.hook: A nervous new voter almost fills in two bubbles for the same office.

facts.fact: Australia has used compulsory voting in federal elections since 1925, and people who do not vote without a valid reason can be fined.
facts.hook: A student comparing countries is surprised that skipping a vote could cost money somewhere.

facts.fact: India has marked voters' fingers with indelible ink based on silver nitrate since its 1962 general election, so no one can vote twice.
facts.hook: A teen sees a photo of a relative abroad proudly holding up an ink-stained finger.

facts.fact: CIRCLE, a research center at Tufts University, estimated that 50 percent of Americans aged 18 to 29 voted in the 2020 presidential election.
facts.hook: Friends argue about whether young people's votes matter when half of them do not show up.

facts.fact: In Canadian federal elections, an eligible voter who is not on the voters list can register at their assigned polling place on election day.
facts.hook: A Canadian teen realizes on election morning that they never registered.

facts.fact: Edward Elgar's Pomp and Circumstance March No. 1, the usual North American graduation processional, premiered in 1901 in Liverpool.
facts.hook: Waiting to walk in, a graduate hums the tune and wonders where it came from.

facts.fact: Pomp and Circumstance became graduation music after it was played at Yale's commencement in 1905, where Edward Elgar received an honorary doctorate of music.
facts.hook: A band member rehearsing the march for the ceremony wonders why every school plays the same song.

facts.fact: Elgar took the title Pomp and Circumstance from Shakespeare's Othello, which mentions the "pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war."
facts.hook: An English-class graduate recognizes the phrase from a play they studied.

facts.fact: The square graduation cap is called a mortarboard because it resembles the flat board bricklayers use to hold mortar.
facts.hook: A graduate struggling to keep the cap on during wind asks why it is shaped so awkwardly.

facts.fact: The word valedictorian comes from the Latin vale dicere, meaning "to say farewell," which is why the valedictorian gives a farewell speech.
facts.hook: A student drafting the graduation speech wonders how to say goodbye without sounding corny.

facts.fact: The word diploma comes from a Greek word meaning "paper folded double," from the earlier practice of folding official documents.
facts.hook: A graduate opens the diploma folder and jokes that the paper inside is not even folded.

facts.fact: Commencement means "beginning"; the word was used for graduation ceremonies because graduates begin a new status, such as being a bachelor or master.
facts.hook: A graduate feels sad that it is ending and a friend points out the ceremony's name means starting.

facts.fact: The US average adjusted cohort graduation rate for public high school students was 87 percent in the 2021-22 school year.
facts.hook: At the graduation party, someone realizes a few classmates who started grade nine with them are not there.

facts.fact: In 2023, US workers aged 25 and over with a high school diploma had median weekly earnings of $899, compared with $708 for those without one.
facts.hook: A relative at dinner tells the graduate what the diploma is worth in dollars.

facts.fact: In 2023, the US unemployment rate was 3.9 percent for workers aged 25 and over with a high school diploma and 5.6 percent for those without one.
facts.hook: A friend who dropped out talks about how hard job hunting has been.

facts.fact: The GED tests were created in 1942 to let military service members and veterans who had not finished high school show high-school-level skills.
facts.hook: A graduate learns that a grandparent earned a GED after serving in the military.

facts.fact: In the United Kingdom, government bills are drafted by lawyers in the Office of the Parliamentary Counsel before being introduced to Parliament.
facts.hook: Students at a model parliament discover that writing a clear bill is harder than arguing for it.

facts.fact: Any member of the US House of Representatives may introduce a bill in the House, and it is then referred to a committee for study.
facts.hook: A student emails their representative asking them to introduce an idea as a bill.

facts.fact: In the UK Parliament, a government bill's first reading is a formality: the bill is introduced without debate or a vote.
facts.hook: On a legislature field trip, students are disappointed that the first reading lasts only seconds.

facts.fact: In Westminster-style parliaments such as the UK's, the second reading is a debate and vote on a bill's general principles, before its details are examined.
facts.hook: A model parliament debate goes off the rails when someone argues about a comma instead of the main idea.

facts.fact: In Westminster-style parliaments, the third reading is the final debate and vote on a bill as amended, after its details have been examined in committee.
facts.hook: A student bill that survived committee changes faces one last vote in the model parliament.

facts.fact: When the US House and Senate pass different versions of a bill, a conference committee of members from both chambers can write a compromise, which both chambers must then pass.
facts.hook: Two student councils pass different versions of the same rule and must agree on one.

facts.fact: Under the US Constitution, if the president neither signs nor vetoes a bill within ten days, Sundays excepted, while Congress is in session, it becomes law without a signature.
facts.hook: A student tracking a bill online wonders why it became law though the president never signed it.

facts.fact: A pocket veto happens when Congress adjourns during the president's ten-day window and the president does not sign the bill, so it does not become law.
facts.hook: A civics class is puzzled that a bill died without the president ever saying no.

facts.fact: Congress can override a US president's veto with a two-thirds vote in both the House and the Senate.
facts.hook: Students count votes to see whether a vetoed bill they care about can still pass.

facts.fact: Since 1975, ending most debate in the US Senate through cloture has required three-fifths of senators, which is 60 votes when all 100 seats are filled.
facts.hook: A student asks why a bill with 55 supporters in the Senate still failed.

facts.fact: Article I, Section 7 of the US Constitution requires all bills for raising revenue to originate in the House of Representatives, though the Senate may amend them.
facts.hook: A student wonders why a tax bill could not start in the Senate.

facts.fact: The last time a British monarch refused royal assent to a bill was in 1708, when Queen Anne vetoed the Scottish Militia Bill.
facts.hook: During a model parliament, someone playing the monarch threatens to reject the bill, and others check whether that is realistic.

facts.fact: Simple interest is calculated as I = P times r times t: the principal, times the annual interest rate, times the time in years.
facts.hook: A teen works out what a small loan from a relative will cost if interest is charged simply.

facts.fact: Compound interest follows A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt), where n is how many times per year interest is added, so more frequent compounding gives a slightly larger total.
facts.hook: Comparing two savings accounts at a credit union, a teen notices one compounds monthly and one yearly.

facts.fact: APY, annual percentage yield, includes the effect of compounding, so a savings rate of 4.65 percent compounded monthly is quoted as 4.75 percent APY.
facts.hook: A teen sees two different percentages advertised for the same bank account.

facts.fact: A credit card's grace period lets you avoid interest on new purchases if you pay the full balance by the due date each month.
facts.hook: A first-time cardholder debates paying the minimum or the whole bill.

facts.fact: Under the US Credit CARD Act of 2009, card statements must show how long it would take to pay off the balance by making only the minimum payment.
facts.hook: A teen reads the fine print on their first credit card statement and gasps at the number of years.

facts.fact: In a fixed-payment loan, each payment's interest is charged on the remaining balance, so early payments go more toward interest and later payments more toward principal.
facts.hook: Someone checks a car loan statement and is dismayed at how little the balance dropped.

facts.fact: At the same interest rate, a longer loan term lowers the monthly payment but increases the total interest paid over the life of the loan.
facts.hook: At a car dealership, a salesperson offers a lower payment by stretching the loan to seven years.

facts.fact: Payment history is the largest factor in a FICO credit score, making up about 35 percent of it for the general population.
facts.hook: A teen who forgot a phone bill payment wonders how much it will hurt their credit.

facts.fact: For US federal Direct Subsidized student loans, the government pays the interest while the student is in school; unsubsidized loans build interest during that time.
facts.hook: A graduating senior compares the two loan offers in a financial aid letter.

facts.fact: Capitalization means unpaid interest is added to a loan's principal, so from then on interest is charged on the interest too.
facts.hook: An older sibling is shocked to find their student loan balance larger than what they borrowed.

facts.fact: The US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau notes a typical payday loan fee of $15 per $100 borrowed for two weeks equals an annual percentage rate of almost 400 percent.
facts.hook: A friend short on rent considers a payday loan until someone does the math.

facts.fact: The US National Labor Relations Act, signed on July 5, 1935, gave most private-sector workers the right to form unions and bargain collectively.
facts.hook: Grocery store workers talk in the break room about whether they are legally allowed to organize.

facts.fact: The US National Labor Relations Act does not cover government employees, agricultural workers, domestic workers, supervisors or independent contractors.
facts.hook: A teen doing farm work in summer finds out the union rules their cousin described do not apply to them.

facts.fact: The US Fair Labor Standards Act took effect on October 24, 1938, setting the first federal minimum wage at 25 cents an hour and a maximum workweek of 44 hours.
facts.hook: A part-timer complaining about pay learns what the very first federal minimum was.

facts.fact: The 1947 Taft-Hartley Act, passed over President Truman's veto, allowed US states to pass right-to-work laws banning contracts that require workers to pay union fees.
facts.hook: Two coworkers who moved from different states disagree about whether they must pay union dues.

facts.fact: Canada's Rand formula, from Justice Ivan Rand's 1946 ruling after a Ford strike in Windsor, Ontario, requires all workers covered by a union contract to pay dues.
facts.hook: A Canadian teen questions why dues come off their paycheck when they never joined the union.

facts.fact: In NLRB v. J. Weingarten (1975), the US Supreme Court ruled that unionized workers may request a union representative at an interview they reasonably believe could lead to discipline.
facts.hook: A unionized kitchen worker called into the manager's office wonders if they can bring someone.
