facts.fact: The US Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that 10.0 percent of wage and salary workers were union members in 2025, down from 20.1 percent in 1983.
facts.hook: A student interviewing a grandparent about work learns unions were far more common decades ago.

facts.fact: In 2025, US union members had median weekly earnings of $1,404, compared with $1,174 for workers who were not union members, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
facts.hook: Two friends at different grocery chains compare paychecks and one store is unionized.

facts.fact: The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire in New York on March 25, 1911, killed 146 garment workers, many trapped because exit doors had been locked.
facts.hook: A new employee notices a fire exit blocked with boxes and remembers a history lesson.

facts.fact: The Haymarket affair in Chicago on May 4, 1886, grew out of protests for an eight-hour workday and is considered the origin of May 1 as International Workers' Day.
facts.hook: A teen wonders why workers march on May 1 in so many countries.

facts.fact: Denmark, Norway and Sweden have no statutory national minimum wage; pay floors are instead set through collective agreements between unions and employers.
facts.hook: Students debating minimum wage are surprised some high-wage countries do not have a legal one.

facts.fact: In a strike, employees refuse to work; in a lockout, the employer stops work by keeping employees out of the workplace.
facts.hook: A teen arrives for a shift to find the doors locked and a sign saying the store has shut out its workers.

facts.fact: Frida Kahlo's The Two Fridas (1939) is a large, nearly square oil painting, about 173 centimetres on each side, showing two seated self-portraits side by side.
facts.hook: A student at a gallery stands back to see how the two figures fill the square canvas.

facts.fact: In The Two Fridas, one Frida wears a white European-style Victorian dress and the other wears a traditional Tehuana dress, a contrast often read as her mixed European and Mexican heritage.
facts.hook: Two friends argue about which of the two Fridas is the real one.

facts.fact: In The Two Fridas, both women's hearts are exposed, and a single blood vessel connects them, winding through their hands and hearts.
facts.hook: A student sketching the composition traces the red line that ties the figures together.

facts.fact: Kahlo painted The Two Fridas in 1939, the year she divorced the muralist Diego Rivera; they remarried the following year.
facts.hook: A student's critique changes once they read the painting's date on the gallery label.

facts.fact: In Kahlo's Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird (1940), the dead hummingbird hanging at her throat is a Mexican folk charm for luck in love.
facts.hook: A student assumes the bird is just decoration until a grandparent explains the tradition.

facts.fact: In Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird, a black cat peers over Kahlo's shoulder, usually interpreted as a symbol of bad luck and death.
facts.hook: A student lists every animal in the painting and asks what each one is doing there.

facts.fact: In Kahlo's The Broken Column (1944), her spine is painted as a cracked Ionic column visible through an opening in her body.
facts.hook: An art student wonders why a Greek column appears inside a human figure.

facts.fact: In The Broken Column, nails pierce Kahlo's face and body while tears run down her cheeks, yet she looks straight at the viewer.
facts.hook: A viewer feels uncomfortable meeting the painted eyes and tries to explain why in their critique.

facts.fact: On September 17, 1925, when Kahlo was 18, a streetcar crashed into her bus, leaving injuries that caused her pain for the rest of her life.
facts.hook: A student realizes Kahlo was their own age when the accident that shaped her paintings happened.

facts.fact: The Surrealist André Breton described Kahlo's art as "a ribbon around a bomb," though Kahlo herself later rejected the Surrealist label.
facts.hook: A student's critique calls Kahlo a Surrealist and a classmate objects.

facts.fact: Complementary colours sit opposite each other on the traditional colour wheel, like red and green, and placed side by side they make each other look brighter.
facts.hook: A student analyzing a Kahlo notices the red and green seem to vibrate next to each other.

facts.fact: The AP 2-D Art and Design portfolio's Sustained Investigation section asks for 15 digital images and counts for 60 percent of the score.
facts.hook: A senior planning a ten-piece portfolio realizes a school requirement needs more images.

facts.fact: The AP 2-D Art and Design portfolio's Selected Works section asks for 5 artworks and counts for 40 percent of the score.
facts.hook: A student agonizes over which five pieces are strongest.

facts.fact: Hokusai's print series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, made around 1830 to 1832, actually contains 46 prints, because ten were added after the first 36 sold well.
facts.hook: A student worried about exceeding ten pieces learns a famous series outgrew its own title.

facts.fact: Cindy Sherman's Untitled Film Stills (1977 to 1980) is a series of 70 black-and-white photographs of herself posed as characters from imaginary movies.
facts.hook: A student planning a self-portrait theme looks for ways to keep ten pictures from looking identical.

facts.fact: Claude Monet painted more than thirty views of the facade of Rouen Cathedral in 1892 and 1893, showing it under different light at different times of day and year.
facts.hook: A student paints the same tree at dawn and dusk and doubts whether it is enough variety.

facts.fact: Monet showed fifteen paintings from his Haystacks series at the Durand-Ruel gallery in May 1891, and most sold within a month.
facts.hook: A student preparing a show wonders whether buyers will want a set of pictures of the same subject.

facts.fact: Josef Albers made over 1,000 works in his Homage to the Square series from 1950 until 1976, keeping nested squares constant while changing only the colours.
facts.hook: A student decides to keep the same composition across the portfolio and change one element.

facts.fact: An artist's statement is written in the first person by the artist to explain the ideas, methods and context behind a body of work.
facts.hook: A student keeps writing about themselves as 'the artist' and a teacher suggests saying 'I'.

facts.fact: Artists commonly keep two versions of their statement: a short one of about 50 to 100 words and a longer one of about 500 to 1,000 words.
facts.hook: A student needs one statement for a gallery wall card and another for an application.

facts.fact: Under US law, an artwork is protected by copyright automatically the moment it is created in a fixed form; registration is voluntary, though needed before suing over a US work.
facts.hook: A student worries that posting portfolio pieces online means anyone can use them.

facts.fact: The overall equation for aerobic cellular respiration is C6H12O6 + 6 O2 -> 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + energy: glucose and oxygen become carbon dioxide and water.
facts.hook: A student at a pond wonders where the carbon in their breath came from.

facts.fact: Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm, outside the mitochondria, and splits one glucose molecule into two pyruvate molecules for a net gain of two ATP.
facts.hook: A student drawing a cell diagram has to decide where to put the first step.

facts.fact: In the mitochondrial matrix, each pyruvate is converted into acetyl-CoA, releasing one molecule of carbon dioxide.
facts.hook: A study group argues about which step makes the first carbon dioxide.

facts.fact: Hans Krebs and William Johnson described the citric acid cycle in 1937, and Krebs shared the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for it.
facts.hook: A student asks why the cycle has a person's name on it.

facts.fact: The journal Nature rejected Hans Krebs's 1937 paper on the citric acid cycle, and he published it in the journal Enzymologia instead.
facts.hook: A student discouraged by a rejected science fair entry hears how one Nobel discovery was first turned down.

facts.fact: The citric acid cycle turns twice for each glucose molecule, because one glucose produces two acetyl-CoA molecules and each enters the cycle separately.
facts.hook: A student's ATP tally comes out wrong until they realize everything after glycolysis happens twice.

facts.fact: The electron transport chain sits in the inner mitochondrial membrane, where oxygen is the final electron acceptor and combines with protons to form water.
facts.hook: A student realizes the oxygen they breathe ends up as water inside their cells.

facts.fact: Peter Mitchell proposed in 1961 that cells make ATP using a proton gradient across a membrane, called chemiosmosis, and won the 1978 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
facts.hook: A student compares the proton buildup to water behind a dam at a farm.

facts.fact: ATP synthase works like a tiny rotary motor: protons flowing through it make part of the enzyme spin, and that motion builds ATP.
facts.hook: At a science museum, a student sees a spinning model and connects it to the mitochondria.

facts.fact: Paul Boyer and John Walker shared the 1997 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for explaining how ATP synthase makes ATP.
facts.hook: A student researching the rotary enzyme finds that working it out earned a Nobel Prize.

facts.fact: When muscle cells run low on oxygen, they convert pyruvate into lactate, which regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue making 2 ATP per glucose.
facts.hook: During a hard sprint across a farm field, a student feels their legs tire and wonders what the cells are doing.

facts.fact: DNA copying is semiconservative: each new double helix keeps one strand from the original molecule and pairs it with one newly built strand.
facts.hook: two students at a science museum argue whether a copied DNA molecule is all new or half old

facts.fact: Before DNA can be copied, the enzyme helicase unwinds the double helix by breaking the hydrogen bonds that hold the base pairs together.
facts.hook: a student unzipping a jacket at a pond uses it to explain to a friend how helicase opens DNA

facts.fact: In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine and guanine pairs with cytosine; in RNA, uracil takes the place of thymine and pairs with adenine.
facts.hook: a student transcribing a DNA sequence for homework keeps writing T in the RNA and has to find the mistake

facts.fact: In transcription, the enzyme RNA polymerase reads one strand of DNA and builds a matching strand of messenger RNA, which carries the gene's instructions.
facts.hook: a student explains to a younger cousin at a farm why a cell makes a working copy instead of sending out the DNA itself

facts.fact: In plant and animal cells, introns are cut out of newly made RNA and the remaining exons are spliced together before the messenger RNA leaves the nucleus.
facts.hook: a student editing a video by cutting out bad takes realises it is like RNA splicing

facts.fact: The genetic code is read in codons of three bases; there are 64 possible codons but only 20 standard amino acids, so most amino acids have more than one codon.
facts.hook: a student checks a codon chart at a science museum and is surprised several codons mean the same amino acid

facts.fact: Translation usually begins at the codon AUG, which also codes for the amino acid methionine.
facts.hook: a student decoding an mRNA puzzle at a science fair starts in the wrong place and gets nonsense

facts.fact: Each transfer RNA carries one amino acid and has a three-base anticodon that pairs with the matching codon on the messenger RNA.
facts.hook: students acting out translation in a community garden hand each other labelled cards as tRNA and codons

facts.fact: In translation, the ribosome moves along the messenger RNA and joins amino acids together with peptide bonds to build a protein chain.
facts.hook: a student compares the ribosome to someone threading beads along a string while reading a pattern

facts.fact: Because several codons can code for the same amino acid, some single-base mutations change nothing in the finished protein; these are called silent mutations.
facts.hook: a student is puzzled that a changed DNA letter in a textbook example leaves the protein exactly the same

facts.fact: Le Chatelier's principle states that when a system at equilibrium is disturbed, the equilibrium shifts in the direction that partly counteracts the change.
facts.hook: a student at home tries to predict what a sealed reaction will do before heating it

facts.fact: The principle is named after the French chemist Henry Louis Le Chatelier, who stated it in 1884.
facts.hook: a student at a science museum finds Le Chatelier's name on a panel and looks up who he was

facts.fact: If the forward reaction is exothermic, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium toward the reactants, because the system absorbs the added heat by running in reverse.
facts.hook: a student's science fair prediction fails because they forgot the forward reaction gives off heat

facts.fact: If the forward reaction is endothermic, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium toward the products.
facts.hook: two friends disagree about which way a heat-absorbing reaction will shift when they warm it

facts.fact: A useful way to predict temperature effects is to treat heat as a product of an exothermic reaction and as a reactant of an endothermic one.
facts.hook: a student at a grandparent's house writes 'heat' into the equation to finally make the problem make sense

facts.fact: Of the common disturbances to an equilibrium, a change in temperature is the only one that changes the value of the equilibrium constant K.
facts.hook: a student keeps using the same K after heating a reaction and gets every answer wrong

facts.fact: Raising the temperature for an exothermic reaction decreases its equilibrium constant, while raising it for an endothermic reaction increases the constant.
facts.hook: a student compares K values in a data table and notices they fall as the temperature rises

facts.fact: Brown nitrogen dioxide forms colourless dinitrogen tetroxide in an exothermic reaction, so a sealed tube of the gas turns paler when cooled and darker brown when warmed.
facts.hook: at a science museum a student watches a sealed tube of brown gas change colour in ice water

facts.fact: Making ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen is exothermic, so low temperatures favour more ammonia at equilibrium, but industrial plants run hotter because the reaction is too slow when cold.
facts.hook: a student asks why a factory would choose a temperature that gives less product

facts.fact: An equilibrium is dynamic: the forward and reverse reactions keep happening, but at equal rates, so the amounts of reactants and products stay constant.
facts.hook: a student compares a busy shop with the same number of people inside all afternoon to a reaction at equilibrium

facts.fact: Raising the temperature speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions, but it speeds up the endothermic direction more, which is why the equilibrium shifts that way.
facts.hook: a student wonders why heat does not just speed everything up equally

facts.fact: The number of moles in a sample equals its mass in grams divided by its molar mass in grams per mole.
facts.hook: a student baking at home realises weighing flour is like weighing out moles of a chemical

facts.fact: The molar mass of a compound is the sum of the molar masses of the atoms in its formula; for carbon dioxide it is 12.01 plus two times 16.00, or 44.01 grams per mole.
facts.hook: a student checking their math at a grandparent's kitchen table forgets to double the oxygen

facts.fact: Table salt, sodium chloride, has a molar mass of about 58.44 grams per mole.
facts.hook: a student weighing salt for a science fair experiment needs to know how many moles are in the bag

facts.fact: The coefficients in a balanced chemical equation give the ratio of moles that react, not the ratio of masses.
facts.hook: a student's product calculation is wildly off because they used grams in the equation's ratio

facts.fact: In the balanced equation 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, two moles of hydrogen gas react with one mole of oxygen gas to form two moles of water.
facts.hook: a student at a science museum counts atoms on both sides of a hydrogen-burning equation

facts.fact: The limiting reactant is the one that runs out first, and it sets the greatest amount of product a reaction can make.
facts.hook: friends making sandwiches run out of bread first and compare it to a limiting reactant

facts.fact: Percent yield is the actual mass of product obtained divided by the theoretical yield, multiplied by 100.
facts.hook: a student's science fair crystals weigh less than predicted and they calculate what went wrong

facts.fact: Molar mass in grams per mole has the same number as a particle's average mass in atomic mass units; one carbon atom averages about 12.01 units, and one mole of carbon about 12.01 grams.
facts.hook: a student notices the same number on the periodic table works for one atom and for a whole mole

facts.fact: One mole of an ideal gas takes up about 22.4 litres at 0 degrees Celsius and 1 atmosphere of pressure.
facts.hook: a student at home fills a box to show how much space a mole of gas would take

facts.fact: The law of conservation of mass means the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants in a closed system.
facts.hook: a student's sealed bag reaction at a science fair weighs the same before and after

facts.fact: In a parliamentary system, the head of government, usually a prime minister, holds office by keeping the confidence of the legislature rather than by winning a separate popular election.
facts.hook: a student at a grandparent's house asks why nobody voted directly for the prime minister

facts.fact: In a presidential system, the president is elected separately from the legislature for a fixed term and cannot be removed simply because the legislature disagrees with them.
facts.hook: two friends at a community centre compare how their countries' leaders stay in office

facts.fact: In many parliamentary systems, a government that loses a vote of no confidence in the lower house must resign or call a general election.
facts.hook: a student watches a news broadcast of a no-confidence vote and asks what happens next

facts.fact: On 28 March 1979, the UK government of James Callaghan lost a vote of no confidence by a single vote, 311 to 310, forcing a general election.
facts.hook: a student learns one vote once brought down a British government and thinks about whether their vote matters

facts.fact: Germany uses a constructive vote of no confidence: the Bundestag can remove a chancellor only by electing a successor in the same vote.
facts.hook: a student in a mock parliament tries to remove a leader without naming a replacement and is told it would not work in Germany

facts.fact: In 1982 Helmut Kohl replaced Helmut Schmidt as German chancellor through a constructive vote of no confidence, the only time the procedure has succeeded at the federal level.
facts.hook: a student researching Germany finds a leader changed without any general election

facts.fact: In the United States, the House of Representatives impeaches a president by a simple majority, but the Senate needs a two-thirds vote to convict and remove them.
facts.hook: at a courthouse tour, a student confuses impeachment with removal and a guide corrects them

facts.fact: In 1868 the Senate acquitted President Andrew Johnson by one vote: 35 senators voted to convict, one short of the two-thirds needed.
facts.hook: a student learns how close a president came to removal and debates whether that is too high a bar

facts.fact: In 2022 the United Kingdom had three prime ministers, Boris Johnson, Liz Truss and Rishi Sunak, without a general election, because the governing party changed its leader.
facts.hook: a student with relatives in the UK is surprised the prime minister changed twice in one year

facts.fact: Many parliamentary systems separate the head of state, such as a monarch or ceremonial president, from the head of government, while in the United States the president is both.
facts.hook: a student at a polling station asks why some countries have both a king and a prime minister

facts.fact: The 22nd Amendment to the US Constitution, ratified in 1951, limits a person to being elected president twice.
facts.hook: a student asks why a popular president cannot just keep running

facts.fact: In France, the directly elected president appoints the prime minister, but the National Assembly can force the prime minister's government to resign by passing a censure motion.
facts.hook: a student comparing systems finds France mixes parliamentary and presidential features

facts.fact: The First Amendment to the US Constitution, ratified in 1791, says Congress shall make no law abridging the freedom of speech.
facts.hook: students preparing for a mock court read the amendment's exact words aloud before choosing sides

facts.fact: The First Amendment limits what the government can do to speech; it does not by itself stop a private employer or private company from restricting speech.
facts.hook: a student claims their free speech rights were violated by a private website and a teammate challenges it

facts.fact: In Schenck v. United States (1919), Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote that free speech would not protect a man falsely shouting fire in a theatre and causing a panic.
facts.hook: a mock court lawyer quotes 'shouting fire' and the other side points out who said it and when

facts.fact: Schenck v. United States introduced the 'clear and present danger' test, allowing speech to be punished if it created a clear and present danger of harm Congress could prevent.
facts.hook: a student arguing for the government tries to use an old test the other side says is outdated

facts.fact: Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969) held that advocating force can be punished only if it is directed to inciting imminent lawless action and is likely to produce such action.
facts.hook: at a mock court, a student has to decide whether an angry speech meets the 'imminent lawless action' test

facts.fact: In Tinker v. Des Moines (1969), the Supreme Court ruled 7-2 that students do not shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech at the schoolhouse gate.
facts.hook: students arguing a school dress-code case look for the most famous line about student speech

facts.fact: In Texas v. Johnson (1989), the Supreme Court ruled 5-4 that burning the American flag as a political protest is protected symbolic speech.
facts.hook: a student assigned to argue against flag burning learns how close the vote was

facts.fact: In West Virginia v. Barnette (1943), the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that public schools cannot force students to salute the flag or recite the Pledge of Allegiance.
facts.hook: a student asks whether they can be made to stand for the pledge and a mock court teammate cites the case

facts.fact: In Mahanoy Area School District v. B.L. (2021), the Supreme Court ruled 8-1 that a school violated a student's free speech by punishing an off-campus Snapchat post.
facts.hook: a student worried about a post made on the weekend researches what the Court said

facts.fact: New York Times v. Sullivan (1964) held that a public official suing for libel must prove actual malice: that the statement was known to be false or made with reckless disregard for truth.
facts.hook: a mock court student argues a newspaper's error about a mayor should not be punished

facts.fact: Cocoa butter can crystallize in six different forms, and tempering aims to make most of it set in form V, the crystal form that gives shine and snap.
facts.hook: a student's homemade chocolate bars come out dull and crumbly and they read up on cocoa butter

facts.fact: Form V cocoa butter crystals melt at about 33.8 degrees Celsius, just below body temperature, which is why well-tempered chocolate melts in the mouth but not in the hand.
facts.hook: friends at a farmers' market wonder why the chocolate stays solid on the table but melts on the tongue

facts.fact: Milk chocolate is usually tempered to a lower working temperature than dark chocolate, around 29-30 degrees Celsius, because milk fat softens the cocoa butter.
facts.hook: a student uses dark chocolate temperatures on milk chocolate and the batch will not set

facts.fact: In the seeding method, chopped chocolate that is already tempered is stirred into melted chocolate to supply form V crystals for the rest to copy.
facts.hook: a friend without a marble slab uses leftover store-bought chocolate to temper a batch

facts.fact: In the tabling method, melted chocolate is spread and worked on a cool marble slab to bring its temperature down and start stable crystals forming.
facts.hook: at a friend's house a student tries tabling on a cold stone counter

facts.fact: Fat bloom is a dull grey or white streaky film that appears on chocolate that was not properly tempered or has melted and reset.
facts.hook: a student finds greyish streaks on chocolate left in a warm car and figures out why

facts.fact: Sugar bloom is a dry, gritty white coating caused when moisture dissolves sugar on the chocolate's surface and the sugar recrystallizes as it dries.
facts.hook: chocolates taken from a cold fridge into a humid room turn powdery on the surface

facts.fact: A few drops of water in melted chocolate can make it seize into a thick, grainy paste, because the sugar and cocoa particles clump together.
facts.hook: steam from a double boiler drips into the bowl and the chocolate suddenly turns stiff

facts.fact: Properly tempered chocolate shrinks slightly as it sets, which helps it release cleanly from a mould.
facts.hook: a student's chocolates stick in the mould and they realise the batch was never in temper

facts.fact: Compound or coating chocolate, which replaces some or all cocoa butter with other fats, sets without tempering but does not have the same snap.
facts.hook: a friend at a campsite uses candy melts and asks why they did not need tempering

facts.fact: The USDA calls 4 to 60 degrees Celsius (40 to 140 degrees Fahrenheit) the danger zone, the range where bacteria in food multiply rapidly.
facts.hook: a student leaves a pot of chili out overnight after batch cooking and a housemate questions it

facts.fact: The USDA advises refrigerating cooked food within two hours, or within one hour if the air temperature is above 32 degrees Celsius (90 degrees Fahrenheit).
facts.hook: friends at a hot campsite debate whether leftovers from lunch are still safe for dinner

facts.fact: The USDA recommends eating refrigerated cooked leftovers within three to four days, which limits how far ahead a week of meals can be cooked without freezing some.
facts.hook: a student plans seven days of batch-cooked lunches and realises the last ones need the freezer

facts.fact: Dividing a large batch into shallow containers helps it cool quickly in the fridge, because a deep pot of hot food stays warm in the middle for hours.
facts.hook: a student at a community kitchen splits a huge pot of soup into flat containers

facts.fact: Freezing food at -18 degrees Celsius (0 degrees Fahrenheit) stops bacteria from growing but does not kill most of them, so thawed food can spoil again.
facts.hook: a student assumes freezing cleaned their leftovers and a friend explains otherwise

facts.fact: The USDA advises reheating leftovers to an internal temperature of 74 degrees Celsius (165 degrees Fahrenheit).
facts.hook: a student uses a food thermometer on reheated batch-cooked rice for the first time

facts.fact: Frozen food can be thawed safely in the refrigerator, in cold water or in the microwave, but not by leaving it out on the counter.
facts.hook: a student forgets to move tomorrow's frozen meal into the fridge and has to choose a safe way to thaw it

facts.fact: Freezer burn happens when air dries out the surface of frozen food; it makes food tough and tasteless but does not make it unsafe to eat.
facts.hook: a student finds white dry patches on frozen stew and has to decide whether to throw it out

facts.fact: Canada's 2019 food guide suggests filling half the plate with vegetables and fruits, a quarter with protein foods and a quarter with whole grain foods.
facts.hook: a student planning a week of meals uses the plate proportions to build a shopping list

facts.fact: The shelf label's unit price shows the cost per gram, litre or item, which lets shoppers compare packages of different sizes fairly.
facts.hook: at the grocery store a student finds the bigger bag of oats is not actually cheaper

facts.fact: A UN Environment Programme report found that 1.05 billion tonnes of food were wasted in 2022, and about 60 percent of that waste happened in households.
facts.hook: a student notices how much of last week's shopping went bad and starts planning meals

facts.fact: In his Poetics, Aristotle said a well-made plot is a whole with a beginning, a middle and an end.
facts.hook: a student's play about a family argument starts and stops without an ending and a friend asks what changed

facts.fact: Gustav Freytag described dramatic structure as a pyramid of exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution in his 1863 book on drama technique.
facts.hook: a student sketches a pyramid on a napkin at drama camp to find where the climax of their play belongs

facts.fact: The principle called Chekhov's gun, from the playwright Anton Chekhov, holds that anything clearly shown on stage early should matter later in the play.
facts.hook: a friend at a table read asks why a letter in the first scene never comes back

facts.fact: Subtext is the meaning beneath what characters actually say, such as anger or love that a line never names out loud.
facts.hook: a student rewrites a scene about a fight with a sibling so neither character says what they really feel

facts.fact: Tennessee Williams called The Glass Menagerie, first staged in Chicago in 1944, a memory play: it is narrated by Tom, who looks back on his family.
facts.hook: a student writing about their own past decides to have a narrator step out and speak to the audience

facts.fact: Tennessee Williams based Laura, the fragile sister in The Glass Menagerie, on his own sister Rose.
facts.hook: a student hesitates to put a real family member in a play and reads how Williams did it

facts.fact: Stage directions in a script are usually set apart in italics or parentheses so actors and directors can tell them from spoken lines.
facts.hook: at a community theatre, an actor reads a stage direction aloud as dialogue at the first read-through

facts.fact: A table read is a seated read-through of a script by the cast, used to hear how the dialogue sounds before any staging begins.
facts.hook: a student hears their play read aloud for the first time and realises a line sounds nothing like how people talk

facts.fact: Dramatic irony is when the audience knows something that a character on stage does not, which lets a short scene build tension quickly.
facts.hook: a student lets the audience see a hidden letter early so the family scene that follows feels tense

facts.fact: In the United States and many other countries, a play is protected by copyright automatically as soon as it is written down, without needing to be registered.
facts.hook: a student worries someone will steal their script before a drama camp showcase

facts.fact: A ten-minute play usually has one setting and few characters, because there is little time to change scenery or introduce many people.
facts.hook: a student's play about a whole summer has six locations and they must choose one moment instead

facts.fact: Blocking is the planned positioning and movement of actors on stage, set by the director during rehearsals.
facts.hook: a student directing a one-act play at a community theatre finds actors bumping into each other in scene two

facts.fact: The word blocking comes from 19th-century directors such as W. S. Gilbert, who planned scenes on a model stage using a block for each actor.
facts.hook: a student director at drama camp uses coins on a table to plan where actors stand

facts.fact: Stage left and stage right are named from the actor's point of view while facing the audience, so they are the reverse of the audience's left and right.
facts.hook: a first-time director tells an actor to move left and the actor goes the wrong way

facts.fact: Upstage means away from the audience and downstage means toward it; the terms come from old raked stages that sloped down toward the audience.
facts.hook: an actor at a community theatre asks why the back of a flat stage is called 'up'

facts.fact: The stage manager records the blocking in the prompt book so that it can be repeated the same way at every performance.
facts.hook: an actor forgets their cross on opening night and the stage manager's notes settle the argument

facts.fact: Spike tape is coloured tape used to mark where furniture and actors should be placed on the stage floor.
facts.hook: a sofa keeps drifting across the stage during rehearsals until a student director marks the floor

facts.fact: Cheating out means an actor turns their body partly toward the audience, even while talking to another character, so their face and voice carry.
facts.hook: a student director notices the audience can only see the back of the lead's head

facts.fact: Countering is when one actor shifts position to balance the stage after another actor crosses, keeping both visible to the audience.
facts.hook: during rehearsal one actor keeps getting hidden every time another walks past

facts.fact: On a stage in the round, the audience sits on all sides, so the director must keep actors moving so no section only sees their backs.
facts.hook: a student's play moves to a room where chairs surround the playing space and the blocking must change

facts.fact: An off-book rehearsal is one where actors must perform without their scripts, having memorised their lines.
facts.hook: a student director sets an off-book date and one actor is nowhere near ready

facts.fact: The Gulf Stream is a warm ocean current that flows out of the Gulf of Mexico through the Florida Straits and north along the east coast of the United States.
facts.hook: a student traces the Gulf Stream on a current map at a science museum with their finger

facts.fact: The Gulf Stream leaves the US coast near Cape Hatteras, North Carolina, and turns northeast across the Atlantic.
facts.hook: a student looking at a current map wonders why the warm arrow leaves the coast at North Carolina

facts.fact: Beyond the Grand Banks of Newfoundland, the Gulf Stream's continuation toward Europe is called the North Atlantic Current or North Atlantic Drift.
facts.hook: a student is confused when the same current changes its name partway across the map

facts.fact: The Gulf Stream's surface speed typically reaches about 2.5 metres per second at its fastest, making it one of the fastest ocean currents.
facts.hook: a student compares the current's speed to walking pace while reading a map at a planetarium

facts.fact: About 30 million cubic metres of water per second flow through the Florida Straits in the Gulf Stream, a flow oceanographers call 30 sverdrups.
facts.hook: a student learns a unit named for an oceanographer and tries to picture that much water

facts.fact: On many ocean current maps, warm currents are drawn with red arrows and cold currents with blue arrows.
facts.hook: a student misreads a current map because they thought the colours showed speed

facts.fact: The ocean stores heat from summer and releases it into the air in winter, and prevailing westerly winds carry that warmth onto northwestern Europe.
facts.hook: a student at a grandparent's house asks why the wind direction matters for a warm current

facts.fact: A 2002 study led by Richard Seager argued that winds and the ocean's seasonal heat storage, more than the Gulf Stream itself, explain most of Europe's mild winters.
facts.hook: a student's report says the Gulf Stream alone warms Europe and a classmate finds a study that disagrees

facts.fact: London lies at about 51.5 degrees north, farther north than any point in the contiguous United States.
facts.hook: a student comparing a map is surprised London is farther north than the US-Canada border

facts.fact: Murmansk, a Russian port north of the Arctic Circle, stays ice-free all year because of warm water carried by the North Atlantic Current.
facts.hook: a student looking at a map asks why ships can reach a port so far north in winter

facts.fact: In the far North Atlantic, the water cools and becomes dense enough to sink, then flows south deep underwater as part of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation.
facts.hook: a student at a science museum sees an animation where the red current turns blue and dives

facts.fact: Benjamin Franklin had a chart of the Gulf Stream printed in London in 1769, using knowledge from his cousin Timothy Folger, a Nantucket whaling captain.
facts.hook: a student learns that ship captains were saving days by avoiding the current long before satellites

facts.fact: Earth's surface gives off heat as infrared radiation; greenhouse gases absorb much of it and re-emit it in all directions, including back down, which warms the lower atmosphere.
facts.hook: At a science museum, a student holds a hand near an infrared camera screen and asks a friend why the glowing heat from the ground does not all escape to space.

facts.fact: Nitrogen and oxygen make up about 99 percent of dry air but are not greenhouse gases, because molecules made of two identical atoms do not absorb infrared radiation.
facts.hook: Studying for a test at a grandparent's house, a student wrongly assumes the most common gases in the air must trap the most heat, and a cousin checks the textbook.

facts.fact: Without its natural greenhouse effect, Earth's average surface temperature would be about minus 18 degrees Celsius instead of roughly 14 degrees Celsius.
facts.hook: At a planetarium, two friends compare Earth with the Moon and argue over whether greenhouse gases are a bad thing or something life depends on.

facts.fact: Charles David Keeling of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography began regular carbon dioxide measurements on Mauna Loa, Hawaii, in March 1958; the resulting graph is called the Keeling Curve.
facts.hook: A student preparing a class presentation has to explain where the famous rising carbon dioxide graph comes from and cannot find the name of the station at first.

facts.fact: The first carbon dioxide reading at Mauna Loa, in March 1958, was about 313 parts per million.
facts.hook: Reading a carbon dioxide graph for homework, a student has to find the starting value on the left edge before calculating how much it has risen.

facts.fact: On May 9, 2013, the daily average carbon dioxide level measured at Mauna Loa passed 400 parts per million for the first time in the record.
facts.hook: At a grandparent's house, a student points to where a carbon dioxide graph crosses the 400 line and a grandparent asks what year that was.

facts.fact: The Keeling Curve zigzags every year because Northern Hemisphere plants take in carbon dioxide as they grow in spring and summer, then release it as leaves die and decay in autumn and winter.
facts.hook: A student reading the Mauna Loa graph thinks the yearly wiggles are measurement errors until a classmate asks what happens to trees each season.

facts.fact: In 1859, John Tyndall began laboratory experiments measuring how gases absorb infrared heat, showing that water vapor and carbon dioxide absorb it while nitrogen and oxygen do not.
facts.hook: A student writing a report assumes the greenhouse effect is a modern idea and is surprised to find a nineteenth-century experiment behind it.

facts.fact: In 1896, Swedish scientist Svante Arrhenius made the first calculation of how much Earth would warm if the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere doubled.
facts.hook: At a planetarium talk, a student asks whether climate predictions only started with computers and a friend looks up the earliest estimate.

facts.fact: Water vapor is the most abundant greenhouse gas, but it acts mainly as a feedback: warmer air holds more water vapor, which amplifies warming started by other gases like carbon dioxide.
facts.hook: During a debate practice, a student claims water vapor, not carbon dioxide, is the real cause of warming, and a teammate has to explain the difference.

facts.fact: Methane traps far more heat per molecule than carbon dioxide, but a methane molecule stays in the atmosphere for only about a decade on average, much less time than carbon dioxide.
facts.hook: Near a rock quarry, a student and a friend argue whether cutting methane leaks or carbon dioxide would slow warming faster in the next few years.

facts.fact: David Ricardo set out comparative advantage in his 1817 book On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation, using England and Portugal trading cloth and wine.
facts.hook: At a farmers' market, a student preparing for an economics exam tries to remember which two countries and goods were in the original example.

facts.fact: In a model with two goods, one country cannot have a comparative advantage in both, because a lower opportunity cost for one good means a higher opportunity cost for the other.
facts.hook: At a grandparent's house, a student insists one country could be better at everything in every sense, and a grandparent asks what each one gives up.

facts.fact: Both countries gain from trade only if the exchange rate between the two goods falls between the two countries' own opportunity costs of making them.
facts.hook: Two stallholders at a farmers' market haggle over how many jars of honey a basket of apples is worth, and a student works out the fair range.

facts.fact: By specializing and trading, two countries can each end up consuming combinations of goods that lie beyond what they could produce on their own.
facts.hook: A student drawing production possibility graphs for homework is puzzled when the trade point lands outside the curve and has to explain how that is possible.

facts.fact: Trade based on comparative advantage raises a country's total income, but individual workers in industries that now face cheaper imports can still lose their jobs or wages.
facts.hook: At a grandparent's house, a student praises free trade and a relative who worked in a closed factory asks who actually gained.

facts.fact: If two countries give up exactly the same amount of one good to make the other, neither has a comparative advantage, and Ricardo's model predicts no gain from specializing.
facts.hook: Working through a textbook problem, a student finds identical ratios for both countries and wonders why the answer says trade would not help.

facts.fact: A lawyer who types faster than her assistant still gains by hiring him to type, because every hour she spends typing is an hour of better-paid legal work given up.
facts.hook: A student running a small tutoring business debates whether to pay a younger sibling to handle scheduling even though the student is faster at it.

facts.fact: The Heckscher-Ohlin model, named after Swedish economists Eli Heckscher and Bertil Ohlin, explains comparative advantage by differences in countries' supplies of land, labor and capital.
facts.hook: At a bank, a student reading about a country with vast farmland asks why it exports grain but imports electronics.

facts.fact: Ricardo's original model treats labor as the only cost of production and assumes that cost stays the same however much of a good is made.
facts.hook: Preparing an essay, a student has to list the simplifying assumptions behind Ricardo's example before criticizing it.

facts.fact: Transport costs shrink the gains from comparative advantage, and if shipping a good costs more than the difference in production costs, trading it no longer pays.
facts.hook: At a lemonade stand, two friends realize that buying cheap lemons from across town is not worth it once they count the bus fare.

facts.fact: In the United States the Federal Reserve's main policy rate is the federal funds rate, the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserves.
facts.hook: At a bank, a student hears a news report say the Fed raised rates and asks a teller which rate the Fed actually sets.

facts.fact: On January 25, 2012, the US Federal Reserve adopted an explicit inflation target of 2 percent, measured by the personal consumption expenditures price index.
facts.hook: Writing an economics essay, a student cannot explain why 2 percent inflation counts as success until finding when the Fed set that goal.

facts.fact: New Zealand was the first country to adopt formal inflation targeting, when its government and Reserve Bank agreed in March 1990 on a target range of 0 to 2 percent.
facts.hook: At a grandparent's house, a student asks whether central banks have always aimed at a set inflation number, and they look up which country started it.

facts.fact: Higher interest rates pay savers more, so households tend to shift some money from spending into savings, which lowers demand for goods and helps slow price rises.
facts.hook: A student with a summer-job paycheck at a bank notices the savings account rate went up and weighs saving versus buying a new phone.

facts.fact: Raising interest rates tends to strengthen a country's currency by attracting foreign savings, which makes imports cheaper and puts downward pressure on prices.
facts.hook: Planning a school trip abroad, a student notices the exchange rate improved after the central bank raised rates and wonders why.

facts.fact: If people trust a central bank to keep inflation low, they ask for smaller wage and price increases, and that expectation itself helps keep inflation down.
facts.hook: At a lemonade stand, two friends debate raising their price because they expect everything else to cost more next month.

facts.fact: US inflation peaked at 14.8 percent in March 1980 and fell below 3 percent by 1983, after the Federal Reserve's sharp interest rate increases.
facts.hook: A student reading an inflation graph for class has to explain the steep drop in the early 1980s to a study partner.

facts.fact: Slowing inflation by raising rates usually costs jobs: during the US recession of the early 1980s, unemployment rose above 10 percent.
facts.hook: At a grandparent's house, a student praises the rate hikes that beat inflation and a relative describes losing a job that year.

facts.fact: The Taylor rule, proposed by economist John Taylor, says that when inflation rises one percentage point a central bank should raise its interest rate by more than one percentage point.
facts.hook: In an economics club, a student argues a central bank only needs to match rising inflation and a friend explains why it must go further.

facts.fact: The US Federal Reserve began raising its policy rate from near zero in March 2022 and reached a range of 5.25 to 5.50 percent in July 2023.
facts.hook: A student helping a parent compare mortgage offers at a bank asks why rates today are so different from a few years earlier.

facts.fact: GIS data comes in two main forms: vector data uses points, lines and polygons, while raster data is a grid of cells, each holding one value.
facts.hook: A student trying to load a flood map and a housing map notices one looks like shapes and the other like pixels, and has to figure out why.

facts.fact: Roger Tomlinson led development of the Canada Geographic Information System in the 1960s, the first computerized GIS, and is often called the father of GIS.
facts.hook: At an airport waiting for a flight to Canada, a student reading about GIS history finds out where the technology began.

facts.fact: In 1854, physician John Snow mapped cholera deaths in London and showed they clustered around one water pump on Broad Street, an early example of spatial analysis.
facts.hook: A student building a GIS project needs an example for the introduction and remembers a famous map that helped stop a disease outbreak.

facts.fact: Landscape architect Ian McHarg's 1969 book Design with Nature promoted stacking maps of soil, water and other factors to decide land use, an idea that GIS later automated.
facts.hook: At a grandparent's house, a student finds old tracing-paper planning maps and realizes they work like the layers in GIS software.

facts.fact: In the United States, a 100-year flood zone does not mean a flood every 100 years; it means the area has a 1 percent chance of flooding in any given year.
facts.hook: Helping a relative look at houses, a student sees a listing inside a 100-year flood zone and the seller claims it is safe for a century.

facts.fact: A home with a 1 percent yearly flood chance has about a 26 percent chance of flooding at least once during a 30-year mortgage.
facts.hook: At home, a student runs the numbers on a family friend's new house near a river and is surprised how high the long-term risk is.

facts.fact: An intersect overlay in GIS keeps only the areas that appear in both input layers, so intersecting housing with a flood zone shows just the homes inside the zone.
facts.hook: A student's first overlay shows every house in the city, and a classmate explains which tool would show only the ones at risk.

facts.fact: A buffer in GIS draws a zone of a set distance around a feature, such as every area within 100 meters of a river.
facts.hook: A student mapping flood risk for a class project wants to include homes near the river even outside the official flood zone.

facts.fact: GIS layers stored in different coordinate reference systems will not line up correctly until one is reprojected to match the other.
facts.hook: At home, a student overlays a flood map on a housing map and finds the river running through the middle of the city hall, a sign something is misaligned.

facts.fact: A digital elevation model is a raster layer storing the ground height of each cell, which GIS uses to predict where water will flow and collect.
facts.hook: A student wonders why some streets far from the river still show flood risk on a GIS map, until checking the elevation layer.

facts.fact: Each feature in a GIS layer links to a row in an attribute table, so data such as the number of residents in each building can be totaled for a selected area.
facts.hook: Presenting to a town meeting role-play, a student needs to say how many people live in the flood zone, not just how many houses.

facts.fact: A population pyramid conventionally shows males on the left and females on the right, with age groups stacked from youngest at the bottom to oldest at the top.
facts.hook: At a travel agency, a student glances at a country profile chart and at first reads the bars the wrong way round.

facts.fact: A pyramid with a wide base and narrow top shows a high birth rate and a young population, pointing to a growing need for schools and teachers.
facts.hook: Researching a volunteer trip, a student compares two countries' pyramids and has to predict which one needs more classrooms.

facts.fact: A pyramid whose base is narrower than its middle shows falling birth rates and an aging population, pointing to rising demand for nursing homes and elder care.
facts.hook: At a grandparent's house, a student looks at their own country's pyramid and wonders who will staff the care homes in twenty years.

facts.fact: In countries with low death rates, a total fertility rate of about 2.1 children per woman is needed to replace the population without migration.
facts.hook: A student reading about their country's falling birth rate cannot see why 2 children per family is not enough to keep numbers steady.

facts.fact: Japan has one of the world's oldest populations, with about 29 percent of its people aged 65 or over in the early 2020s.
facts.hook: At an airport, a student flying to Japan for an exchange reads about the country's pyramid and wonders how that changes daily life.

facts.fact: Niger has one of the highest birth rates in the world, so its population pyramid has a very wide base and a large share of children.
facts.hook: Comparing pyramids for class, a student sees one that looks like a steep triangle and has to explain what it means for schools there.

facts.fact: The dependency ratio compares people aged under 15 and 65 and over with people aged 15 to 64, estimating how many dependents each working-age person supports.
facts.hook: At home, a student tries to explain to a parent why an aging population could mean higher taxes for workers.

facts.fact: On a pyramid with five-year age groups, a bulge moves up one bar every five years, so today's large group of babies becomes a large group of schoolchildren soon after.
facts.hook: Planning a presentation, a student has to predict when a town's recent baby boom will hit the local high school.

facts.fact: The United States baby boom generation was born between 1946 and 1964, and its bulge on the pyramid has now moved into the retirement ages.
facts.hook: At a grandparent's house, a student realizes the grandparents are part of the bulge on the pyramid chart for homework.

facts.fact: The top of most population pyramids has more women than men, because women live longer than men on average.
facts.hook: Reading a pyramid for class, a student notices the right side is wider at the top and a friend at home guesses why.

facts.fact: Migration can reshape a pyramid: some Gulf states, such as Qatar, show a large bulge of working-age men because many foreign male workers live there.
facts.hook: At an airport, a student looks at a Gulf country's pyramid for a school project and thinks the chart has an error.

facts.fact: A blood pressure reading gives two numbers in millimeters of mercury: systolic pressure when the heart beats, over diastolic pressure when the heart relaxes between beats.
facts.hook: At a pharmacy, a student tries the free blood pressure machine and has to explain to a grandparent what the top and bottom numbers mean.

facts.fact: Under the 2017 American College of Cardiology and American Heart Association guideline, normal adult blood pressure is below 120 systolic and below 80 diastolic.
facts.hook: At a doctor's office, a student reads 118 over 76 on a chart and wonders whether that counts as good.

facts.fact: Under the 2017 American guideline, elevated blood pressure means a systolic reading of 120 to 129 with a diastolic reading below 80.
facts.hook: At a pharmacy, a parent's reading comes out 125 over 78 and a student checks what category that falls into.

facts.fact: Under the 2017 American guideline, stage 1 hypertension means a systolic reading of 130 to 139 or a diastolic reading of 80 to 89.
facts.hook: At a grandparent's house, a student looks at a home monitor log and has to decide whether to suggest a doctor's visit.

facts.fact: Under the 2017 American guideline, stage 2 hypertension means a systolic reading of 140 or higher or a diastolic reading of 90 or higher.
facts.hook: At a doctor's office, a student sees a relative's reading of 142 over 88 and wonders why the nurse calls it stage 2 when the bottom number seems fine.

facts.fact: High blood pressure often causes no symptoms at all, which is why it is called a silent killer and is found mainly by measuring it.
facts.hook: At a grandparent's house, a grandparent says they feel fine so their pressure must be fine, and a student questions that.

facts.fact: White coat hypertension is when blood pressure reads high in a clinic, often from nervousness, but normal at home, so doctors may check it with home or all-day monitoring.
facts.hook: At a doctor's office, a nervous student's reading is high, and the doctor asks about home readings before drawing any conclusion.

facts.fact: The DASH diet, short for Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension, was tested in a US trial funded by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute and published in 1997.
facts.hook: Helping a grandparent plan meals after a doctor's visit, a student looks up what the diet the doctor named actually stands for.

facts.fact: The World Health Organization recommends adults eat less than 2 grams of sodium a day, which is less than 5 grams of salt, to help lower blood pressure.
facts.hook: At a grandparent's house, a student reads the sodium label on a can of soup and adds up how quickly the day's limit is reached.

facts.fact: Regular aerobic exercise, such as brisk walking or cycling on most days, lowers blood pressure in many people, including those who already have hypertension.
facts.hook: A student at a pharmacy encourages a parent with a high reading to join evening walks and they plan a schedule together.

facts.fact: For an accurate reading, a person should sit quietly for about five minutes with feet flat and the arm supported at heart level, because posture and activity change the numbers.
facts.hook: At a pharmacy, a student rushes in and uses the machine right away, then gets a much lower reading after sitting a few minutes.

facts.fact: Consent to sexual activity must be freely given and can be withdrawn at any time, including after activity has already started.
facts.hook: In a health class role-play set at a doctor's office, a student asks whether saying yes earlier means a person cannot change their mind.

facts.fact: The legal age of consent differs by country and even between US states, and in many places it falls between 16 and 18.
facts.hook: At a grandparent's house, a student reading a news story about a law in another country is surprised it differs from home.

facts.fact: Condoms are the only common contraceptive method that also reduces the risk of sexually transmitted infections.
facts.hook: At a pharmacy, a student with a birth control prescription asks the pharmacist whether it also protects against infections.

facts.fact: With typical use, about 13 in 100 people relying only on male condoms for a year have an unintended pregnancy, mostly because condoms are not used correctly every time.
facts.hook: In a health class, a student is surprised that a method rated highly on the box has a much higher real-world failure rate.

facts.fact: With typical use, about 7 in 100 people relying on the combined birth control pill for a year have an unintended pregnancy, often because doses are missed.
facts.hook: At a doctor's office, a student asks why the nurse stresses setting a daily phone reminder for the pill.

facts.fact: Hormonal IUDs and contraceptive implants fail in fewer than 1 in 100 users a year, because once placed by a clinician they do not depend on daily use.
facts.hook: At a clinic, a student compares options with a nurse and learns why long-acting methods are more reliable in practice.

facts.fact: Emergency contraceptive pills work mainly by delaying ovulation, and they are more effective the sooner they are taken after unprotected sex.
facts.hook: A student helps a worried friend find a pharmacy and they learn from the pharmacist why waiting a few days would be a mistake.

facts.fact: Chlamydia and gonorrhea often cause no symptoms, so testing is the only reliable way for a person to know whether they have one.
facts.hook: A student who feels fine wonders whether a clinic test is necessary, and a nurse explains why feeling fine is not proof.

facts.fact: The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that everyone aged 13 to 64 be tested for HIV at least once as part of routine health care.
facts.hook: At a doctor's office, a student is offered an HIV test at a checkup and is surprised it is routine.

facts.fact: All 50 US states and Washington, DC allow minors to consent to testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections without a parent's permission, though some states set a minimum age.
facts.hook: A student who wants to get tested at a clinic worries a parent must sign a form, and a nurse explains the law.

facts.fact: Edmund Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France, published in 1790, condemned the Revolution for destroying tradition, and set the conservative view that historians after 1800 argued with.
facts.hook: At a history museum, a student preparing a historiography essay debates whether to start with a book written before 1800.

facts.fact: Adolphe Thiers's History of the French Revolution, published from 1823 to 1827, praised moderate leaders such as Mirabeau and Lafayette and condemned radicals such as Robespierre.
facts.hook: A student at a historic site in Paris notices a statue of Thiers and discovers he wrote history before he ran France.

facts.fact: Thomas Carlyle's The French Revolution: A History, published in 1837, stressed the moral choices of individuals rather than impersonal historical forces.
facts.hook: At a grandparent's house, a student finds an old copy of Carlyle's book and struggles with its dramatic style while taking notes.

facts.fact: In The Old Regime and the Revolution, published in 1856, Alexis de Tocqueville argued the Revolution continued the centralization of power already begun under the French monarchy.
facts.hook: At a historic site, a student notices that royal government buildings were reused after 1789 and connects it to Tocqueville's argument.

facts.fact: Socialist politician Jean Jaurès wrote a socialist history of the French Revolution in the early 1900s that shaped the class-conflict interpretation dominant for much of the twentieth century.
facts.hook: A student at a war memorial sees Jaurès's name, learns he was assassinated in 1914, and then finds he was also a historian.

facts.fact: Georges Lefebvre's 1939 book, translated as The Coming of the French Revolution, described 1789 as four revolutions: aristocratic, bourgeois, urban popular and peasant.
facts.hook: Struggling to organize an essay, a student borrows Lefebvre's idea of several revolutions at once to structure a paragraph.

facts.fact: Marxist historian Albert Soboul argued the Revolution was the moment the bourgeoisie overthrew feudal society and became the dominant class.
facts.hook: At a history museum, a student reads a label calling 1789 a bourgeois revolution and wonders whose interpretation that is.

facts.fact: Alfred Cobban's 1954 inaugural lecture at University College London, published in 1955 as The Myth of the French Revolution, attacked the Marxist social interpretation.
facts.hook: A student outlining an essay needs to name the moment when historians first seriously challenged the Marxist view.

facts.fact: François Furet's 1978 book, translated as Interpreting the French Revolution, argued the French should stop treating the Revolution as the key to all of modern French history.
facts.hook: At a grandparent's house, a student explains to a relative why historians in the 1970s stopped agreeing about 1789.

facts.fact: Lynn Hunt's 1984 book Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution turned attention to symbols, language and festivals as sources for understanding the Revolution.
facts.hook: At a history museum, a student studies a revolutionary poster and realizes images can be evidence for an essay, not just decoration.

facts.fact: Simon Schama's Citizens, published in 1989 for the Revolution's bicentenary, argued that violence was an essential part of the Revolution from 1789 onward.
facts.hook: Two students at a historic site disagree over whether the Terror was a detour or built into the Revolution from the start.

facts.fact: Orthodox or traditionalist historians of the Cold War, writing mainly in the late 1940s and 1950s, blamed its outbreak chiefly on Soviet expansion in Eastern Europe.
facts.hook: At a history museum, a student reads an old exhibit panel and wonders why it puts all the blame on one side.

facts.fact: William Appleman Williams's 1959 book The Tragedy of American Diplomacy began the revisionist school, arguing that American economic expansion helped cause the Cold War.
facts.hook: At a grandparent's house, a student is surprised to find an American historian who blamed the United States for the Cold War.

facts.fact: Gar Alperovitz argued in Atomic Diplomacy (1965) that the atomic bombs were used on Japan partly to intimidate the Soviet Union.
facts.hook: At a war memorial, a student and a friend argue whether the bombings of 1945 were the last act of World War II or the first act of the Cold War.

facts.fact: John Lewis Gaddis's 1972 book The United States and the Origins of the Cold War, 1941-1947 argued that neither side could bear sole responsibility, a view called post-revisionism.
facts.hook: Preparing for a debate, a student looks for a historian who blamed both sides and finds the term post-revisionist.

facts.fact: In We Now Know, published in 1997 after Soviet archives had partly opened, Gaddis placed much more responsibility on Stalin personally for the Cold War.
facts.hook: A student comparing two Gaddis books notices the same historian changed his mind and has to explain why in an essay.

facts.fact: After the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, some Soviet archives became available to researchers, giving historians evidence about Stalin's decisions that earlier writers never had.
facts.hook: At a history museum, a student asks why historians writing in the 1990s could be more confident than those of the 1960s.

facts.fact: The Venona decrypts of Soviet intelligence messages, released by the US government in 1995, confirmed that Soviet spy networks had operated in the United States.
facts.hook: Weighing two historians' claims, a student realizes one wrote before 1995 and could not have seen the decrypted spy messages.

facts.fact: Winston Churchill said in a speech at Fulton, Missouri, on March 5, 1946, that an iron curtain had descended across Europe.
facts.hook: At a war memorial, a student hears a guide quote the iron curtain line and checks where and when it was actually spoken.

facts.fact: The Truman Doctrine, announced in March 1947, pledged US support for countries resisting communist pressure, starting with aid to Greece and Turkey.
facts.hook: A student building a Cold War timeline at a grandparent's house argues over whether this speech or the Long Telegram marks the start.

facts.fact: Melvyn Leffler's A Preponderance of Power, which won the 1993 Bancroft Prize, argued US leaders pursued national security through dominance of the postwar world.
facts.hook: Writing an essay comparing historians, a student needs a second view to set against Gaddis and finds Leffler's prize-winning book.

facts.fact: The Soviet Union refused Marshall Plan aid and pressed Eastern European governments, including Czechoslovakia, to withdraw after first showing interest.
facts.hook: At a history museum, a student sees a map of Marshall Plan countries and asks why Eastern Europe is blank.

facts.fact: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus says that if F is an antiderivative of f, then the integral of f from a to b equals F(b) minus F(a).
facts.hook: At home, a student about to add up hundreds of rectangles realizes an antiderivative gives the exact answer in two steps.

facts.fact: The antiderivative of x to the power n is x to the power n plus 1, divided by n plus 1, for every n except negative 1.
facts.hook: At a math club meeting, a student tries the power rule on 1 over x and gets division by zero.

facts.fact: The area under the curve y equals x squared, from x equals 0 to x equals 1, is exactly one third.
facts.hook: At a grandparent's house, a student estimates the area under a parabola with graph-paper squares and then checks it with an integral.

facts.fact: The antiderivative of 1 over x is the natural logarithm of the absolute value of x, which fills the one gap the power rule leaves.
facts.hook: At a tutoring centre, a student stuck on the integral of 1 over x learns why the logarithm appears.

facts.fact: A Riemann sum approximates the area under a curve by adding up the areas of thin rectangles, and the integral is the limit as the rectangles become infinitely thin.
facts.hook: At home, a student uses a spreadsheet to add more and more rectangles under a curve and watches the total settle.

facts.fact: Bernhard Riemann gave his definition of the integral in 1854, in the paper he submitted to qualify as a lecturer at the University of Göttingen.
facts.hook: Writing a short math history report, a student looks up whose name is on the rectangle method and when it was defined.

facts.fact: Gottfried Leibniz introduced the integral sign in 1675, basing it on an elongated letter s because he thought of an integral as an infinite sum.
facts.hook: At a tutoring centre, a younger student asks why the integral sign looks like a stretched letter, and the tutor explains its origin.

facts.fact: In a definite integral the constant of integration cancels out, because it is added to both F(b) and F(a) and then subtracted away.
facts.hook: At home, a student loses marks for leaving plus C on a definite integral answer and works out why it does not belong.

facts.fact: The area between two curves is found by integrating the upper function minus the lower function over the interval where they are ordered that way.
facts.hook: At a math club meeting, two students get different areas between a line and a parabola because one subtracted in the wrong order.

facts.fact: Integrating a velocity function over a time interval gives the displacement, which is the area under the velocity-time graph.
facts.hook: Driving with a grandparent, a student reads the speedometer every minute and later estimates the distance traveled with an integral.

facts.fact: The power rule says the derivative of x to the power n is n times x to the power n minus 1, so the derivative of x cubed is 3x squared.
facts.hook: a student checking a friend's homework notices every answer forgot to lower the power by one

facts.fact: The derivative of a constant is zero, so adding 7 to a function shifts its graph up but leaves its derivative unchanged.
facts.hook: two students get different functions but the same derivative and argue about who made the mistake

facts.fact: The derivative of a function at a point equals the slope of the line tangent to its graph at that point.
facts.hook: a math club member lays a ruler along a curve on graph paper to check a computed derivative

facts.fact: At a local maximum of a polynomial the derivative equals zero, because the tangent line at the top of the peak is horizontal.
facts.hook: a student sketching a profit curve realizes the highest point is where the slope flattens out

facts.fact: A zero derivative does not guarantee a maximum or minimum: f(x) = x cubed has derivative zero at x = 0, but its graph keeps rising through that point.
facts.hook: a student confidently labels a point a maximum and a tutor asks them to graph the function first

facts.fact: By the second derivative test, if f'(a) = 0 and f''(a) is negative, the function has a local maximum at x = a.
facts.hook: a student unsure whether a critical point is a peak or a valley differentiates a second time to find out

facts.fact: By the first derivative test, a point where the derivative changes from positive to negative is a local maximum, because the function rises and then falls.
facts.hook: a student makes a sign chart on a napkin at a grandparent's kitchen table to settle an argument

facts.fact: On a closed interval, a function's largest value can occur at an endpoint where the derivative is not zero, so the endpoints must be checked as well.
facts.hook: a student loses marks on a quiz for finding the critical point but never testing the ends of the interval

facts.fact: The notation dy/dx for a derivative comes from Gottfried Leibniz and is still standard in mathematics today.
facts.hook: a student asks why the textbook writes the derivative as a fraction when it is not really one

facts.fact: Sonata form has three main sections: the exposition presents the themes, the development works them through other keys, and the recapitulation brings them back.
facts.hook: a student marks a Mozart score with three coloured sticky notes before a concert

facts.fact: In a major-key movement in sonata form, the exposition's second theme is usually in the dominant key, so a movement in C major moves to G major.
facts.hook: a student hears a new tune arrive and checks the score to see what key it has moved to

facts.fact: In a minor-key sonata-form movement, the exposition's second theme usually moves to the relative major, such as E-flat major in a movement in C minor.
facts.hook: a student expects the second theme of a minor-key movement to be in the dominant and is surprised

facts.fact: In the recapitulation, the second theme usually returns in the home key rather than the dominant, so the movement ends settled in the key where it began.
facts.hook: a student compares the same theme in two places in the score and spots the key change

facts.fact: In Classical-era sonata-form movements, the exposition is often marked with repeat signs, so the performer plays it twice before the development begins.
facts.hook: a friend following a recording thinks the pianist has made a mistake by starting over

facts.fact: The transition, or bridge, is the passage in the exposition that modulates from the home key to the second key, and it often uses busier, less tuneful material.
facts.hook: a student cannot decide where the first theme ends until they find the passage that changes key

facts.fact: The development typically breaks the exposition's themes into short fragments and moves them quickly through several keys, which gives the section its restless sound.
facts.hook: a student recognizes a few notes of the opening tune hidden inside a stormy middle section

facts.fact: Near the end of the development, a retransition often dwells on the home key's dominant chord, building an expectation that the tonic and the first theme are about to return.
facts.hook: at a concert, a student leans forward because the music sounds as if the opening tune is about to come back

facts.fact: A coda is an optional closing section after the recapitulation that reinforces the home key and brings the movement to an end.
facts.hook: a student's markings run out before the music does and they must name the extra final passage

facts.fact: In Mozart's Piano Sonata in C major, K. 545, the first movement's recapitulation begins unusually in F major, the subdominant, instead of the home key of C major.
facts.hook: a student marks the recapitulation in the wrong place because the first theme returns in an unexpected key

facts.fact: Mozart's works are identified by K numbers from the catalogue compiled by Ludwig von Köchel, first published in 1862.
facts.hook: a student at a concert hall asks what the 'K.' printed after the title in the programme means

facts.fact: In a time signature, the top number gives the number of beats in each bar and the bottom number gives the note value that gets one beat, so 4/4 means four quarter-note beats.
facts.hook: a student's written melody has five beats in some bars and a friend asks what time signature it is in

facts.fact: In standard notation, vertical bar lines divide the staff into bars, also called measures, and a final double bar line with one thick line marks the end of a piece.
facts.hook: a student counts the bar lines to check that their melody really has sixteen bars

facts.fact: Melodies are often built from four-bar phrases, so a sixteen-bar melody commonly falls into four phrases.
facts.hook: a student stuck on a long melody splits it into four short sections to finish it

facts.fact: The three primary chords of a major key are built on its first, fourth and fifth notes, so in C major they are C, F and G.
facts.hook: a student with limited guitar skills plans a whole melody around just three chords

facts.fact: An authentic cadence, a V chord moving to the I chord, sounds final, which is why melodies usually end their last phrase with it.
facts.hook: a friend at a community centre says a student's melody does not sound finished

facts.fact: A half cadence ends a phrase on the V chord, which sounds unfinished and makes the listener expect another phrase to follow.
facts.hook: a student deliberately ends the eighth bar on an unresolved chord to keep listeners waiting

facts.fact: A plagal cadence moves from the IV chord to the I chord and is often called the 'Amen cadence' because many hymns sing 'Amen' to it.
facts.hook: a grandparent hums the end of a hymn and a student recognizes the chord change from class

facts.fact: On a lead sheet, chord symbols such as C, Am or G7 are written above the staff to show which chord accompanies each part of the melody.
facts.hook: a pianist friend asks a student to add the chords above the melody so they can accompany it

facts.fact: The key signature of G major has one sharp, F-sharp, which applies to every F in the piece unless an accidental changes it.
facts.hook: a student's melody sounds wrong when played because they forgot the sharp in the key signature

facts.fact: The treble clef is also called the G clef because its curl circles the second line of the staff, marking that line as the G above middle C.
facts.hook: a student copying a melody by hand draws the clef in the wrong place and the notes shift

facts.fact: In C major the dominant seventh chord is G7, made of the notes G, B, D and F, and it pulls strongly toward the C major chord.
facts.hook: a student adds one note to a chord before the final bar and the ending suddenly feels stronger

facts.fact: A dot after a note adds half the note's value, so a dotted half note lasts three beats in 4/4 time.
facts.hook: a student's bar comes out one beat short until they add a dot to a long note

facts.fact: Between two parallel charged plates, the electric field strength equals the voltage across them divided by the distance between them, written E = V/d.
facts.hook: a student at a science fair has to explain the field in their homemade capacitor to a judge

facts.fact: Two parallel plates 0.02 metres apart with 100 volts across them produce an electric field of 5,000 volts per metre between them.
facts.hook: a student forgets to convert centimetres to metres and gets an answer a hundred times too small

facts.fact: Electric field strength can be measured in volts per metre or in newtons per coulomb, and the two units are equivalent.
facts.hook: two students get the same number with different units and argue about who is right

facts.fact: Between large parallel plates the field is nearly uniform, so away from the edges a point near one plate has the same field strength as a point midway between them.
facts.hook: a student wastes time measuring the distance to each plate before realizing the position does not matter

facts.fact: The electric field between charged plates points from the positive plate toward the negative plate, the direction a positive charge would be pushed.
facts.hook: a student's diagram has the field arrows backwards and a friend asks which way a proton would move

facts.fact: The force on a charge in an electric field equals the charge times the field strength, F = qE, so doubling the charge doubles the force.
facts.hook: a student uses the field they just computed to find the push on a charged dust particle

facts.fact: Near the edges of real plates the field lines bulge outward and the field weakens, an effect called fringing, so E = V/d holds best near the centre.
